About this work

Polygraphiae libri sex — "Six Books of Polygraphy" — is Trithemius's systematic cryptographic manual and the first printed book on the subject in the West. He completed it late in life — the dedication to Emperor Maximilian I is dated 1508 — and it appeared in print only after his death, in 1518. Where the companion Steganographia hides its cipher beneath angelic conjurations, the Polygraphiae is openly didactic: it teaches the craft in plain language, walking the reader from simple substitution alphabets through transposition grids and the famous "Ave Maria" cipher, in which any plaintext is recast as a grammatical Latin prayer. Its sixth book culminates in the polyalphabetic tabula recta — the rotating-alphabet table that anticipates the Vigenère cipher by the better part of a century.

This is the 1550 Frankfurt edition (BSB scan), one of three print witnesses of the Polygraphiae in this corpus (alongside the 1518 and 1600 editions). Composed 1508; printed posthumously 1518; this witness 1550. The Latin was re-OCR'd from the page scans with a vision model and translated by GPT-5.5, with a Fable 5 review pass recovering the cipher tables that a first pass tends to flatten. The cipher apparatus carries a dedicated cipher-key and cipher-grid rendering set beside the source facsimile; the cipher itself is decoded on the cipher solutions page.

Graph. 24° = 4° 83. Trithemius

Six Books of Polygraphy, by Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Peapolitani, formerly of Sponheim, addressed to Emperor Maximilian.

There has been added one book, the Key to Polygraphy, by the same author.

Contained in these books is the method by which one person can communicate to another whatever he wishes, not only secretly, but sometimes even without suspicion. They also present a method most useful both in teaching and in learning. In addition, they provide the capacity for understanding the deepest mysteries of the arts and disciplines.

Explanations of several passages have also been added, especially of those in which the principles of the admirable work Steganography lie hidden; these indeed offer ingenious persons an occasion for discovering things far greater and subtler. By the very learned man Adolph von Glauburg, patrician of Frankfurt.

Frankfurt, 1550.

Munich

To the Divine Emperor Maximilian: the letter of Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Saint James at Würzburg, concerning Polygraphy.

I was wavering in mind, most unconquered Emperor Maximilian, and was somewhat uncertain within myself whether I would be doing something worthwhile if I dedicated the manuscript of our Polygraphy to your imperial majesty. For among the great you are the greatest, among the more powerful the most powerful, and among any wise men by far the wisest; for that reason nothing should be inscribed to you unless it is great, nothing addressed to you unless it has been worked out with the highest learning. But I, having attained no literary learning, or very little, hesitated for quite some time, not without reason, over whether I ought to present my trifles to so great a majesty, since I am neither suited by talent to elaborate anything nor adorned with the necessary charm of speech. For I know, and cannot deny, how scanty my store is, how rough my talent, and how there is in me no vein of eloquence for speaking. Therefore, after due consideration, I stopped for a while, and as an inept writer I feared to appear before your glorious majesty. For since, after God, you are by right lord of the world,

it is no wonder if I, an unlearned man and the least of monks, fear the judgment of so great a majesty as yours and am afraid to offer those compositions of mine which I know are not worthy of your hands. And while I was turning these matters over in my mind, a messenger arrived with letters sent by your highness, in which you summoned me to Cologne, the expenses necessary for the journey having already been sent earlier through another. But when I had read your serenity’s letter, confidence at once overcame modesty, and consideration of your innate gentleness drove fear away. For I know your nature to be most mild: since you are the most modest of all, you are accustomed both to be gentle to the humble and to resist the proud. You do not know how to be vainly puffed up, nor, in the manner of tyrants, to despise the humble who are devoted to your highness, since just as you have no further height to which you may rise on earth, so no envy will penetrate your mind. You are greatest; you have also accomplished many great things, no less bravely than wisely, both in peace and in war. By these you have gained an everlasting name, and with reverence for the highest honor you are celebrated by the love and favor of all your subjects. These are the riches of princes: the love and favor of the people, and doing justice to each according to the commandment of God’s charity. Therefore, since all carry your name to the stars with praises, and everyone proclaims you most mild and most humane, why should I suppose that you in particular would be more severe toward me? From then on there was no reason,

no reason, especially since you deign by your letter to entice me to write. Therefore, at last encouraged by the weighing of these matters, [unclear]

But because your Caesarean majesty, occupied with many affairs, does not have time to examine the things that lie wrapped in mysteries, lest you be deprived of the fruit of my labor, I have appended a little explanatory book for the whole work, which I have designated the key of Polygraphy; with it as guide you will more easily understand all the things concealed here beneath figures. May God preserve you unharmed for our salvation. Written on the twenty-sixth day of the month of April, in the year of Christ 1508.

TABLE, OR INDEX OF THE LUCUBRATIONS OF JOHANNES TRITHEMIUS, FIRST ABBOT OF SPANHEIM and afterward of Saint James of Würzburg.

Johannes Trithemius, abbot, was born in the village of Trittenheim, in the diocese of Trier, on the banks of the river Moselle, on the first day of the month of February, at the eleventh hour and the thirtieth minute after midday, in the year of the Lord’s nativity 1462, in the tenth indiction of the Romans: his father was Johannes de Heidenberg, and his mother was called Elisabeth de Longuico. This was the same year, namely, in which the city of Mainz, in the dissension of two pontiffs, was captured, lost its liberty, and found servitude, many of its citizens having been driven into exile; in the fourth current year of Pope Pius, the second of that name, and the twenty-second of the emperor Frederick III. In the year of the Lord 1482, however, in the monastery of Spanheim in the diocese of Mainz, on the first day of February, the very day on which he had once been born, he laid aside secular dress and there took up the monastic habit under the rule of the divine father Benedict, according to the observance newly introduced. In the following year, which was the eighty-third above the four-hundredth and the thousandth, when Abbot Johannes de Colenhusen had been transferred by canonical postulation to Seligenstadt, Johannes Trithemius, by the common election of the brothers, was promoted and ordained abbot of the aforementioned monastery of Spanheim on the fourth day before the Kalends of July, and presided for twenty-three years, one month, and nineteen days. When these had passed, not without many labors, provoked by the rashness of certain rivals, he accepted the abbey of Saint James of Würzburg, which was being offered to him, and of his own will resigned Spanheim, full of useless cares. In both places he wrote many little works, from which he recently recorded for me in his own hand, on a sheet, the following.

Since you, as a friend, ask me for their titles, I gladly comply with your wishes, so that from consideration of such great labors by our common friend and teacher you may hold his memory more closely. First, then, I shall record the titles of those lucubrations which he laboriously composed while he was abbot at Spanheim. First he wrote the constitutions of his order which were made in the provincial chapters by command of the presidents: one book. On the Visitation of Monks: one book. On the Manner of Holding a Provincial Chapter: one book. On the Rule of Saint Benedict: two books. Homilies and Exhortatory Sermons to His Monks: two books, which he dedicated to his predecessor. On the Temptations of Cloistered Persons and Their Remedies: two books. To Nicolaus, Priest of Mernica, on the Priestly Life: one book. Against the Private Property of Monks: one book. A Penthic Work, that is, a mournful work On the Ruin of His Order: one book. On the Illustrious Men of His Order: four books. Praises of the Order of the Carmelite Brothers: two books. To Gerlacus, Abbot of Deutz, Praises of Manual Scribes: one book. To Johannes Dalburgius, Bishop of Worms, On Ecclesiastical Writers: one book. On the Praises of Saint Anne, Grandmother of the Lord: one book. Chronicle or Annals of the Monastery of Hirsau: two large volumes. Chronicle of the Succession of the Dukes of Bavaria and the Counts Palatine, to Philip, Count Palatine and Elector: one book. Life of Saint Irmina, nun and first abbess in Oeren at Trier: one book. On the Misery of Cloistered Prelates: two books. Praises of Saint Andrew the Apostle: one book. Praises of the Monastic Life: one book. Praises of True Penitence: one book. Monocollogion of a Man Devoted to God to Himself: one book. On the Miracles of the Holy Mother

of the mother Anne, one book. To Ulrich, canon of Cologne, on questions in the Gospel of John, one book. To the same, on questions concerning the Psalms, one book. For the presidents of the annual chapter on the Bursfeld observance, he abridged the statutes of that same union, one book. A Spiritual Exercise for Monks, one book. An epitome or breviary of the same, one book. On the Ecclesiastical Computus, one book. On the Illustrious Writers of Germany, to Jakob Wimpfeling of Sélestat, one book. Letters from Sponheim to various persons, four books. Orations delivered in chapters and elsewhere, twenty-four in number, which make one book. He wrote sermons to his brothers of the monastery of Sponheim, forty in number and very fine, one book. Sermons to the people on feast days, one book. Several supplicatory prayers to God and the saints, one book.

And from the Greek language he translated into Latin Maximus the abbot, On the Incarnation of the Lord; also the anathemas of Saint Cyril, archbishop of Alexandria, promulgated against heretics in the third synod of Ephesus; and certain letters of that same synod. He also wrote for the edification of monks a notable work, which he entitled On the Threefold Region of Cloistered Men, three books. He also wrote certain other smaller works, whose titles he did not indicate to me.

These, most loving brother Nicolaus, are the Trithemian works which, during the twenty-three years in which he was abbot, he composed at Sponheim for the honor of God, amid cares and the continual management of household affairs, reading or writing day and night whenever he was able to steal some leisure for himself. During the years in which he presided he brought into the Sponheim library a very great treasure of books in every field, not only printed by the art of printing but also manuscripts. For when I was with him for the space of one year, to learn Greek and Hebrew letters from him, I counted two thousand volumes in the library, of which at least eight hundred had been suitably written by pen on parchment and paper. I often heard from his own mouth that he had spent more than two thousand florins on books, which he had not taken from the substance of the monastery, which was always very meager, but since he was known to and beloved by many princes,

he spent, for the most part, on books the gifts with which he was honored by them. For he is the greatest lover and cultivator of books above all those whom I know living today in the flesh. It is said by many, however, that his successor, who is now abbot at Sponheim, has alienated many volumes; whether this is true, I certainly do not at all know.

In the year of the Lord 1504, when a fierce war had broken out between the kingdom and Philip, count palatine, Trithemius, from fear of the enemy, withdrew with his library and the monastery’s goods to Kreuznach, the nearest town, and I likewise returned to my own affairs. But in October of the year 1506, Trithemius himself, stirred by the injury done by certain men, accepted the abbacy of Saint James at Würzburg and resigned that of Sponheim. There, in quiet, he is writing various works, whose titles, at my request, he has lately sent on to me.

To Maximilian Caesar he published a marvelous work, which he entitled Polygraphy, six books. To the same, the Key of the same Polygraphy, one book. Answers to Eight Questions of the same Caesar, one book. To the same, On the Seven Intelligences Moving the Spheres, one book. To Joachim, margrave of Brandenburg and prince elector, two books of various questions, orations, and propositions. To the same, On Prognostications Lawful and Not Lawful for a Christian, two books. To the same he wrote that marvelous and laborious work of Steganography, eight books, which that rash Bovillus, not understanding it, censured most ignorantly and most falsely. To the same prince, a book of letters, one book. To the same, Against Malefactors and All Arts and Superstitions Prohibited by the Church, five books. To the same, On the Causes and Cure of the Falling Sickness and of Maleficences, three books. To Jacob Trithemius his brother, An Itinerary of His Life, two books. To Burkhard von Horneck, physician, On the Peculium of Nuns, one book. He wrote a history or annals concerning the origin, kings, and deeds of the people of the Franks and Germans, three large volumes, beginning the narrative from King Marcomer, who in the year 433 before the incarnation of the Lord led the people from the borders of Scythia into Germany, to the mouths

to the mouths of the Rhine, down to the twenty-ninth year of Maximilian Caesar. To Laurentius, bishop of Wurzburg and duke of Eastern Franconia, he wrote an epitome or breviary of those same three volumes of histories, three books. To the same man, On the Dukes and Bishops of the Franks of Wurzburg, one book. On the miracles shown at the memorial of our Lady Saint Mary at Dettelbach, two books. On the miracles of the same Lady shown in the nettle-field at Heilbronn, six books. An Apology against Carolus Bovillus, who slandered what he did not understand, one book. On the Origin and Kings of the Franks, one book. A Chronicle of his own monastery, over which he now presides, Saint James at Wurzburg, one book. To Albert, of the margraves of Brandenburg, archbishop of Mainz and Magdeburg, The Life of the divine Rabanus, archbishop, three books. On the translation of the same man from Mainz into Saxony, one book. To the same man, The Life of Saint Maximus, bishop, one book. To Johann, count palatine, duke of Bavaria, and count in Sponheim, resident at Simmern, On the Origin, Kings, and Dukes of the Bavarians, together with the Counts Palatine and the Counts of Sponheim, four books. He has in hand a laborious work On Demons and Profane, Maleficent, and Superstitious Arts, which will have twelve books; in these he casts out, confounds, and overturns all the tricks of the diabolical arts. Letters from Wurzburg, which he wrote in that abbey, four books.

He also wrote many other smaller works, suited to his own devotion and that of his friends, such as offices, a rosary, the office of the Mass, and various prayers, together with prose sequences on Saint Anne, grandmother of our Savior. He also wrote praises, prayers, and a rosary on Saint Mary Magdalene; a rosary on Saint Joseph, foster-father of the Lord; a rosary on Saint Peter the Apostle; a rosary on Saint John the Evangelist. At the request of Johann, archbishop of Trier, he wrote a sequence on Anne, which begins, “Jesus, King of the heavens,” to the melody “Ave praeclara”; another, to be sung on her feast, which begins, “Let them rejoice on this day”; a third, for the provincial of the Carmelites at Augsburg, beginning, “Let us exult in honor”; a fourth, on Saint Hildegard the virgin, which begins thus, “Praise be to you, Lord, King of eternal glory”; a fifth on Saint

Rupert, duke of the people of Bingen, which begins, “Let them rejoice on this day”; a sixth on Saint Joseph, foster-father of the Lord, which begins thus, “Let us sing, illustrious men”; a seventh on Saint Rabanus, archbishop; an eighth on the wounds of Christ, which begins thus, “Let us adore Jesus Christ; let us mourn him crucified”; a ninth on the compassion of Blessed Mary ever virgin, which begins thus, “Come, let us weep with pious mind, sharing the compassion of the blessed Virgin Mary,” to the melody, namely, “Ave praeclara”; a tenth on Saint Joachim, father of our Lady, which begins thus, “Let us adore the Trinity, let us praise together the Unity, of Father, Son, and Spirit”; an eleventh on the good angel proper to each person; a twelfth for the proper Mass of each priest; a thirteenth on Saint Maximus, bishop of Mainz; a fourteenth on Saint Mary the Virgin, Christ’s hostess; a fifteenth on Saint Mary Magdalene; a sixteenth on Saint Mary of Egypt; a seventeenth on Saint James the Greater, apostle; an eighteenth on Saint Andrew the Apostle; a nineteenth on Saint Benedict, abbot; a twentieth on All Saints. And for each of the named commemorations and saints he composed individual new offices of the Mass, conforming to the divine Scriptures.

He also wrote a little work of meditations and prayers on the Lord’s incarnation, nativity, life, passion, and death, suitable for devotion, two books. The Mirror of Heavenly Doctrine, of no small service to compunction of mind, one book, which begins thus, “The beginning of human salvation.” He also composed many most devout meditations and prayers on our Lord Jesus Christ, on his most holy mother the Virgin Mary, and on various saints, in beautiful variety, along with many other large works, which all devout posterity will see and admire. These, my dearest Nicolaus, are the volumes of our abbot Trithemius, which for nearly thirty years he has written continuously in night study, apart from those still unfinished and in hand, under the hammer, unknown to me. Farewell, from my house at Durlach, on the fifth day of the month of October, in the year of our salvation 1515. Johannes Durlachius.

From the letter of Johannes Durlachius, his disciple, to Nicolaus Hamerius of Emel.

Preface of Johannes Trithemius, abbot of Saint James at Wuerzburg, to Emperor Maximilian, on the Polygraphia.

We read that many of the wise men of old, philosophers, kings, and princes, once devised various and manifold methods by which they might safely entrust to their messengers, when sending them to more distant places, the secrets of counsel and whatever hidden mystery had to be confided, so that they might be fit to carry them and secure from every assault of wicked men, lest either the simplicity of the cabalists should lay bare the mystery, or the inborn curiosity of the bacutii should bring harm to apostolic matters.

Among these, the great Caesar Augustus of the Romans, wishing in difficult affairs to use the obscure service of messengers, changed the breathings of conceived speech from clear forms into dark ones; and by a fine invention, through the dance of metathesis, he made their barbarity, though resistant to his wishes, conform to his command. And this receptive and, as it were, permanent order, nevertheless subject to intention and to the calculation of time, although it keeps messengers safe on the road from the attack of the bacucei, yet, since it does not keep within its regulated bounds, will make all who look on anxious with suspicion of the matter.

Archimedes of Syracuse, easily the foremost of mathematicians, affixed all around a white bird suited to his arrangements, bare at head and feet, with a staff cut straight into the form of a tetragon; and, when the attendants had been arranged in due proportion, he entrusted the work to the winged instrument, until the image of the white bird appeared changed into a magpie. When this had been properly completed, he loosened with his own hand what had been fastened; and when he had allowed it to fly away, there was suddenly a great separation among the familiar faces of the inner chambers, and soon there arose the image of a tortuous

monastic staff, formerly a far too wandering monster, at the sight of which no one could think what it was. Nor did the quarrel of the owls come to rest before the master's image had skillfully tied the magpie again to a similar tetragon.

Marcus T. Cicero, the eloquent orator, using both talent and art, changed the small elements of expression into signs, and set the industrious device, or character, of his intention in place of the customary phrase. Indeed, in this very novelty he used such abundance that his invention could suffice for nearly all things in the world. To these heralds of mysteries the discipline of the art gave a wonderful agility, so that, contrary to the nature of all things, they may serve, solid and intact, the good will of their master. A king can always use their service very safely, though not without great labor and the manifest suspicion of the bucacei.

Cyprian, the most holy bishop and martyr of the church of Carthage, wishing to provide for the benefit of Christians, considerably enlarged the very lessons of the Ciceronian system, and added what had been lacking for our customs.

Pharamund also, the forty-third after Marcomer, most powerful king of the Franks in Germany, when in the year of the Lord's birth 424 he powerfully entered the borders of the Gauls, bound foreign minutiae to his secrets, so that everything might be done safely.

Clodius Crinitus, his elder son, succeeding his father in the kingdom of the Franks, after he had violently subjected all Gaul to his rule, ordered all the Gauls, as conquered men and slaves, to be shorn and their beards shaved; but he commanded the Franks, conquerors and masters of the Gauls, to grow their hair and beard. From this he was called Crinitus. In imitation of his father he wrapped the mysteries of counsel in signs both his own and foreign.

Charlemagne by surname, the sixty-third king of the Franks after Marcomer, who was the first of the Franks to rule the Romans as emperor, with Nanno the grammarian as his teacher, wished to embellish the German language, which was his native tongue, with grammars after the model of Latin. He began an arduous work, which, however, being entangled in many affairs and overtaken by death, he did not complete. He bound owls to various and many minutiae, by which [unclear] greater born Brabant.

Or Namur: Germany had no greater man. To each prefect of the kingdom he assigned, by his art, individual owls. The Northmen, having gone out from the territories of Gothia, when they once cruelly laid waste Gaul, summoned owls from Greece and prepared a safe hiding place for their secrets, which today is known to few.

Our Bede, a monk in England, not ignorant of the Northmen’s deed, described many inventions of the ancients similar to these, by which they made an obscure path clear for mysteries. He was the first to commend artrology to the memory of posterity, and he invented dactylogy. There were some who distinguished small particulars by visible accidents; by their prudence night was turned into day, and without the service of owls light shone in darkness. Concerning these things, the illustrious count palatine, prince-elector, once an eager inquirer into our Steganography, received from us a manifest proof of the method.

Others, multiplying small particulars by regulated division, after the manner of barbarians, overturned the figures of nature, making secret in darkness the dances of shadows coming to birth; and where the secret nature of counsel required it, they supplied cabala to the absent through diapyric devices.

In these matters there is great labor and a long exercise of the mind over many years, in which no one suddenly becomes expert for use. Necessity sustains everything. There were also some whom celestial harmony taught to compose foreign words; for those who understood them their use was twofold, since one suspended the sense, the other raised it into an ethereal mind. God can do all things. Many tried to seek light in shadow without light, but they could not at all, because the fire lies buried in the ashes. Some practiced painters of masks distinguished one wind into two exactly: one of them, a misophos, always lurks in darkness; the other, a lover of light, a philosophos, hates darkness, loves light, and guards the secret with an owl. Again, as Bede bears witness, there were some whose purpose, advancing to broader things, bound what is invisible to the eyes with visible things, and compelled many plants, and no less stones and shrubs, which lack voices, to speak with a human tongue.

Why should I bring in brute animals, when all things obey the art? This secret is rightly preferred to all inventions up to now; through it the hidden things of mysteries receive strength

and power. Yet reason commands that what is great be hidden under what is small, and that pearls by no means be entrusted to swine. Nothing is brought back from nothing. The known multitude of visible things is great; but invisible things remain remote from us. If the latter are prudently fitted to the former, the enlightened mind of a human being will know and behold marvelous things. But to treat more fully of these matters is not part of the present purpose; since they are greater and weightier, they require another work and another time.

Matthias, the most powerful king of Hungary and a hammer of the Turks harder than adamant, who in our age fought many victorious battles against the enemies of the cross of Christ, discovered many things by marvelous talent and art. He adorned owls with periphrastic devices, held his mysteries secret with manifold variety, and by manifest industry destroyed the counsels of his enemies. He preferred wisdom to gold; therefore he always triumphed as a glorious victor.

In a wise man there is a sound mind in a well-governed body; driven upward by desire for a higher understanding, when through the likeness of the binary you return from the ternary into unity, thereafter you will easily rise to the denary. Pythagoras of Samos, that philosopher, admonished his disciples not to forget the quaternary, in which the first perfection of numbering is comprised. For thus we count: one, two, three, four. Stay your mind; for you have ten. The denary is the head of perfection. What are eleven, except ten and one? What is twenty? Twice ten. What is forty? Four times ten. You have a hundred, and you have by no means departed from the quaternary. And what is a hundred, except ten times ten? Deep mysteries lie hidden in these things, and they are manifest to few.

For love of brevity we shall pass over many in silence, who, aiding nature by art, applied prudence to secrets, and what seemed impossible to many who did not know, brought by shrewd study into easy use. A cultivated mind can do great things, and whoever adheres to God becomes, in understanding, higher than the world. Many are the mysteries of kings, and their counsels are full of cares; in them trust and fidelity are required. Rare fidelity harms the one who believes, and doubt, even when present, often admits it. Therefore it would be worth the effort for all princes to be philosophers, and endowed with singular wisdom, just, gentle, benevolent, and distinguished for munificence, so that they themselves would wish no harm to others

that they themselves should not wish to deceive others, nor easily be able to be supplanted by others. Justice alone, the companion of prudence, makes a prince glorious. At the urging of the aforementioned prince and lord elector, Philip, Count Palatine and Duke of Bavaria, I, Johannes Trithemius, now abbot of the monastery of Saint James at Würzburg, but then of Saint Martin the bishop at Sponheim in the diocese of Mainz, began to write eight books of mysteries in steganography. While I was already continuing my night work on the third book of the same work, something happened which, if I can do so briefly, I am about to relate.

In the year of the Lord’s nativity 1499, in the second Roman indiction, Arnold Bostius, a Carmelite of the town of Ghent, asked me by letter what new work I was bringing forth and with what studies I was occupied. On the day after Palm Sunday, through merchants, I wrote back to him as to a friend, saying that I had under the hammer a new and marvelous work of steganography, and I disclosed in order what was contained in each of the books. But before my letter had reached Ghent, Bostius, during the days of Easter, passed from life to Christ. The prior of that place received the letter, opened it, read it, and, astonished, as I think, by the novelty of the promises, shared it, at the request of many others, to be read and copied. From this it happened that my letter itself, within a short time published through almost all Germany and Gaul and rather often copied by many people, turned even many very learned men to amazement and wonder, to such a degree that they were uncertain what they ought truly to think about me.

Among these there were some who steadfastly declared that my promises in the said letter were frivolous, impossible, and false, and had been shamelessly devised by me for the sake of empty glory. Others, however, said: “This abbot Trithemius promises great and marvelous things; if he can do them, he can do them only by the ministry of demons, since they seem to far exceed the bounds of nature. But if he cannot, who will doubt that he is a liar and rightly to be refuted by all good and learned men?” But let both charges be far from me, since I promised natural things. Yet among all those who rashly judged what they did not know of mine, at last there burst forth into public view as the most rash and most unjust estimator of matters Charles de Bovelles, a Picard by birth, who, after traveling through the upper parts of Alsace, to

for the sake of hospitality he had come to me in Spanheim, intending to return through Trier into Gaul. I treated him with such kindness as I could, and, as long as he was with me, showed him all the benefits of hospitality with a cheerful face. And since, as often happens among friends, especially those devoted to letters, I had shown all my things to my most welcome guest for him to see, among the rest the aforesaid work of Steganography also came forward, not yet at that time completed. Bovelles saw it and read it cursorily, his mind occupied elsewhere; he said that he admired the invention, praised it, and did not trouble himself about the manner in which it was to be understood. Therefore, since he did not ask for the key of understanding, he deserved to hear or perceive nothing of what was contained in that work of ours.

After this, having returned to Gaul, he repaid me evil for good and shamefully violated the covenant of Christian friendship. For when Lord Germain de Ganay, our common friend and later bishop of Orléans, asked him what he had found and seen at my house in Spanheim, he wrote back falsehoods instead of truths and lies instead of benefits, condemning and rashly judging things that he was in no way able to comprehend with his understanding. For since he believed that the palm of learning would be conferred upon him by envy and falsehood, he wrote back to that most learned man a letter filled with falsehood, lies, injuries, and many insults, in which, making mention of a Steganography that he had not understood, he falsely, mendaciously, and with excessively injurious rash presumption proclaims me devoted to evil arts, a magician and necromancer.

By God’s mercy, I shall shortly answer his most mendacious injuries and blasphemies in a brief letter, so that all posterity may understand both that I am innocent and that Bovelles is, in this matter, an impious, cruel, rash liar. I affirm steadfastly, I speak truthfully, and I swear confidently upon my soul that I have never had any commerce with demons or with evil or pernicious magical or necromantic arts; but that all and each of the things that I have either written or promised that I would write are pure, sound, natural, and in no respect at all contrary to the Christian faith. Therefore I do not fear to submit my promises for examination before good and learned men, whenever and as often as there is need, and I do not in any way intend to resist their determination. As to why I have inserted this story of Bovelles’s rashness into this preface of mine, there was a reasonable cause:

so that everyone may understand that it was done by mature counsel that the work of Steganography has remained until now buried in darkness, not because I fear the rash judgments of Bovelles, but lest I should seem to give many others like him cause to suspect similar things about me. Indeed, as far as I am concerned, I would rather appease my rivals by silence than irritate them with letters or provoke them to madness with writings. For I judged it better to consign all wondrous inventions to perpetual silence than, even by the false estimation of men, to incur the mark of magical or necromantic and pernicious superstition. Let Steganography, then, lie hidden in darkness, and let it not become common property for the lying company of Bovelles, which is accustomed to judge matters unknown to it and to corrupt the reputation of a good man from the mere lust of depravity.

Nevertheless, at the urging of friends, so that our rivals, together with Bovelles, may understand how rash and lying an injury he has done us, while Steganography remains within its own limits, we have agreed to bring into the light the work set forth below, which we call Polygraphy, divided into six books. Let those who wish read, and let friends read this volume without bitterness; when they have understood all its hidden mysteries, let them themselves be judges, without envy, whether they are natural or superstitious. For I know, and am certain, that all things are sincere, pure, natural, and far removed from every pursuit of evil superstition.

Whenever, however, the discourse becomes rather obscure, this is done for the reason that a madman should not misuse, to destruction, the sword of defense which a man sound in soul and mind carries for his own protection. Yet nothing evil is contained in it on that account, since perverse men also abuse good things for evil. Whoever presumes to condemn this edition of ours is himself conscious and witness that he has never truly understood it. Mysteries are concealed under enigmas, lest the secrets of owls be made in any way manifest to blockheads. If anyone takes pleasure in knowing these things, let him approach as a reader with envy put far away.

For I am a Christian; I am a priest under the rule of the divine father Benedict and a monk. I love Christ, and with such sincerity of mind as I can, I always adore him devoutly. I have no commerce with demons, I have had none, and, with God as protector, I shall have none; I have no studies, no teachings, in magical or profane arts. Whoever thinks otherwise of me, [unclear]

he thinks wrongly, does an injury, and defends the open falsehood of Bovillus. But now let us dismiss these matters, and set out in order what is contained in each book of our Polygraphy.

TABLE OR INDEX OF THE THINGS that are treated in the first book.

In the first book of this Polygraphy of ours, we arrange and distribute the words of the Latin language, as many as appear there, in the order of our ternary system. By their use and service, princes throughout the world will find safe assistance in any secret matters; without danger to the mystery, without any mark, and without suspicion from owls, it will remain perpetually hidden. By these means the way is known to be safe even for owls, and never to be violated by anyone’s investigation. Knowledge of the hidden matter is granted to two persons only, if the binary is skillfully brought back to the monad. Ignorance is the mother of error, and one who scorns learning the good that he does not know loves blindness.

The periphrases themselves are set forth in the manner either of one advising or of one entreating, and can be varied for every visible subject in this world. For they are suitable to individual mysteries, and are set before Greek secrets no less than before our own. When you have understood the things that you see, do not rashly despise the hidden things that you do not see. You see the accidents; the substance remains invisible. Thus the greater things lie hidden, the lesser lie open to those who look. Since this has been done with reason, let no good man take it for evil, since from these things any suitable person may advance to higher matters, provided that he wishes to do so.

For my part, it has not pleased me on this occasion to pour forth higher things into the light, since an unsuitable time seems to stand in the way. I have set the letters of the Latin alphabet in order before the individual words with this consideration: that the operator may have an easy method in the proposed task, and that the correspondent in the reply may be relieved of excessive labor. The paraphrases that are placed outside the straight order of the lines

are not devoid of the mystery of the art, since they serve luminous propositions for the completion of the necessary perfection, not obscure ones. Therefore they are also taken up in the former and neglected in the latter. For they themselves are the sure means by which every suspicion of an opponent is removed. All things have been set down with reason, so that not even one proposition is introduced idly.

For example, the farther the sun advances from the equinoctial circle, the more the days are lengthened for those who dwell in those regions. Therefore, so that unity may advance in right order through the ternary into the binary, the pattern that we hand down must be observed with the greater care. First, then, after prior consideration, let the intelligent operator of his intention observe what he is to accomplish by the ternary through the binary; let him divide the day with the night into minutes, and distinguish the small divisions of the winds not by another’s assumption of phrasing, but by his own.

In every mystical operation let him carefully beware lest he overturn the established order of the art, substitute one paraphrase for another, or assign to one what is due to another; otherwise unity does not admit the binary, and the whole operation will be confused and useless. Let the night not wander with excessive length, nor advance unsteadily beyond the limits established for it by the art; let curiosity not change water into snow; and let not the man sleep by day who keeps watch by night. Let the mind, alert in intellect, also make use of art, lest the hand by its own levity commit an error which, slight and small in the monad, is accustomed always to appear great and very large in the binary.

One paraphrase from any given order is admitted only into the service of the secret. According to the example of the servant, whenever a small particle of the day’s light demands it, let one phrase likewise adhering to it be taken up, not several. These things must be entrusted to a vigilant mind, and one must beware lest the wind be animated. After this a rule is prescribed for the person approaching the practice of the art: as far as he can by the mystical art, let him imitate the single person of a human being, consisting firmly of two natures, namely the soul, which surpasses visible things, and the flesh, which remains visible. For just as the soul is not seen, although it is placed in a visible body, so the secret of the mind, in order that it may remain secret and nevertheless operate at will, requires the guidance of light while continuing in its workshop of darkness. Therefore, whenever the body serves the soul, the servant the master, the will reason,

see that the principal power of the paraphrase’s potency is preserved in its natural vigor in the light. By this teaching, the first of the Peripatetics will enter duly into the second, and the monad into the binary.

Next, we likewise advise the person who wishes to proceed that, whenever a leaf is moved by the wind, he should discern the property of each nature, compare the night itself with the day by degrees and minutes, and conform the darkness to the light. But if Phoebus should prejudice the night, or the night the sun, by which a confusion of eclipse would arise, either let unity take back the binary which it dismissed in the light, or let the shadow of night be reduced to the first line of the sun. Keep fixed in memory whatever has been produced anywhere in number, weight, and measure.

Therefore, when you have encountered the knot of the difficulty just mentioned, number the minute portions of the night, note also the paraphrases of the daylight, and so blend one from the other that the necessary proportion may follow the action. Beware lest, while an eclipse of the sun endures, you interrupt the necessary labor. Pay no less attention to remembering the ancient fathers: Thuyścon, who was the grandson of Noah and father of the Teutons, and Marcomer, who is read to have been the first to lead the people of the Franks from the borders of Scythia into Germany, to the mouths of the Rhine. For the Franks are brothers of the Greeks and were mingled with the Germans, once making two languages from one. Hence, according to the oracle, those who have lost one g receive g.g.g.

Finally, diligent inquirer into Polygraphy, you are warned that after you, eager for these inventions like one thirsty for water, have attained the true method of operation, you should guard all these things with foresight and not pour them out indiscriminately into the knowledge of all people, especially filthy men. For this reason do not ask, since you know that there is nothing in the world so good and holy that the wicked do not very often abuse it for evil.

NOTICE OF THE THINGS THAT ARE TREATED IN THE SECOND BOOK OF POLYGRAPHY.

In the second book of Polygraphy, nothing new is composed beyond the first, in which only the paraphrases of the word are varied. Therefore whatever we said must be observed in that book, we likewise warn must be kept in this one. For the symbols of both books are composed in the same order under the path of light:

I N T H E R P O L I C I A M V N D E F U R C I A M V N T I C I A M F U R C I A V N T I C I M F U R C I M V N T I C A M F U R CIAM V N TICIA VM FURCIM TVNC FURCIAM TVNC FURCIA VM TVNC TVNC FURCA VM TVNC TVNC FURCIA VM

arranged, and necessarily altered only in the meaning of the paraphrases. In both books, according to the capacity of human understanding, manifold progressions can be made, when the words are varied by metathesis. The pheronomata too are changed at will, whenever the minutes are converted into whole degrees. When this has been done, a wholly marvelous work will arise in the art, and the world, produced by image, will stand in the light, and there will be no fear at all of the Bacuceans in the operator.

I could have given these matters a more beautiful appearance if I had approached the writing of them because I was induced either by some hope of profit or by the use of some advantage of my own. But since none of these things induced me to write, it seemed enough to have given those who desire it an opportunity and material to add more polished things to my discoveries, and to adorn art with art.

INDICATION OF THE THINGS THAT ARE CONTAINED IN THE THIRD BOOK OF THE POLYGRAPHIA.

In the third book of the Polygraphia, having crossed by rational counsel the boundaries of our prescribed nation, we are led to foreign things; and, though placed essentially in the midst of the Franks, we wander farther abroad through the images and likenesses of barbarians. For with almost four thousand mythological paraphrases set in order by art, we show an exceedingly easy way for artificial unity, through which it will securely communicate symbolic notions to its binary at all times. Here the binary is harder than unity; and unless our philologist has become sharp-sighted through prudence, he will make the binary contrary to the monad. For only the ternary, which proceeds from unity and the binary, as a palindrome connects each within itself. But if the usefulness of necessary reasoning is extended beyond the limits of the proposed matter, then the paraphrases are to be counted by minutes from the beginning of the day as often as needed, until the minutes establish the degree in which night is equal to day. The face of this image knows perpetual silence, and does not fear the deceptions of the Bacuceans. It is extended in whatever abundance you wish, and is varied without number.

SMALL INDEX, OR PINAX, OF THE THINGS THAT ARE TREATED IN THE FOURTH BOOK.

In the fourth book of the Polygraphia we place much trust in the binary; after all obstacles have been removed, we have brought it back to unity at first glance, without the labor of difficulty. Hence in this place we use a circle in great matters, a line or point in the smallest. Nor does it matter if night surpasses day, or if light does not agree with darkness, because a circle receives no end, and fullness does not admit emptiness. For they are contraries, and whenever they succeed one another, one is corrupted by the other.

A singular mystery useful to the binary is handed down in this fourth book of the Polygraphia, when the airy wind itself, the composer of the basis, is never designated in anything other than the binary. But in that part the lightness of owls is always suspect to us in difficult matters. The construction of this matter makes paraphrases out of infinite atoms.

INDEX, OR PINAX, OF THE THINGS THAT ARE TREATED IN THE FIFTH BOOK.

In the fifth book of the Polygraphia we have inscribed in two tables, in order, the letters of the Latins, which we Germans also use; one of these is called the straight table, and the other is named the reversed table. Under these we have placed windy orchemata, so that what we seek with labor in foreign things, we may see without difficulty in our own. For besides those things which have been set down by us openly, many more secrets still lie hidden in the inner parts; through understanding these, a path to greater things is opened for the operator, though they are by no means set before everyone. We have also subjected letters to numbers, by which hidden things may be made manifest according to our will. Hence, through the knowing operation of this book, all messages are safely handed over to the Cabalists, although the mysteries are not free from suspicion of the Bacuceans. For every form of metathesis of signs generates suspicion in the one who looks upon it, although it brings no harm to the owls. But you who have attained the understanding of this work will easily penetrate every metathesis of letters among our people and among the Latins.

INDI[unclear]

A Small Index or Summary of the things contained in the sixth book

In the sixth, which is the final book of our Polygraphy, after introducing a mental narration, we have set out in order the minute details of almost all the preceding signs and degrees, and, with arithmetical distributions, have drawn together the functions of the letters into the service of cabalistic operation. One thing lies hidden here in the bark, and another is found in the common operation of the signs. For just as the spirit in the blood gives life to the human body, so the vigor hidden in the art commends the operation. Therefore, for anyone to whom knowledge of this invention is necessary, let him open the eyes of his understanding, so that he may comprehend what the property of each operation is. For we desire all things to be open to good men in such a way that, if it were possible, they would never become manifest to the wicked. A cause compelled us to adapt the letters of the Latins to numbers, lest, if we were too obscure, the intention of our mind should be clear to no one. Yet this novelty, so that it would not be made public without reasonable cause, had to be hidden mystically under unfamiliar signs and marks of numbering. For the nocturnal winds are always stronger than the diurnal, and just as night intercepts day in its own order, so light shudders at darkness. What nature denies, no one dares successfully. We ask the reader not to despise this laborious work of ours before he understands it, but, so that he may be a judge without rashness, let him prudently remove the bark, so that he may come through to the hidden kernel. The work is good and natural, and can be turned to good use or bad, according as the desire of each person’s will is moved. The sword is a good instrument, and it too is turned to good use whenever it is carried for defense without injury to one’s neighbor. But if it is extended unjustly to the injury of anyone, a good thing is loosened into evil through abuse. Therefore, so that the good may have something by which they may prudently provide for their affairs, the Polygraphy is written by us; and so that an opportunity for wrongdoing may not be furnished to the depraved, the kernel is hidden in the bark under various enigmas. The man who is good does not abuse a good thing for evil; rather, if he can, he converts evil into good.

What the causes and at the same time the uses of this work of ours, the Polygraphy, are.

Indeed we undertook the labor of the present work, both rare and difficult, for no other reason than to provide for the usefulness of those in need. I say those in need not of food, not of drink, but of aid in preserving mysteries without danger. We judge, therefore, that it will be worth the effort if we briefly note the uses and advantages that can come to those who use these inventions of ours. For indeed, since we have no business in our personal affairs such that we need these teachings for concealing secrets, we have certainly labored for those whose command had to be obeyed. The first use is that, once the understanding of this work has been completed, it gives an easy method by which you will safely, secretly, and without any suspicion on the part of any observers make known the secret of your mind to an industrious person who knows the art, as widely as there may be need, over any distance of places governed by speech.

What lies hidden in these things, the work of Steganography draws out, which requires neither letters nor a messenger who knows the secrets he carries. It would be otherwise in matters that admit the light, according to the common custom of all our people. Do not take the matter otherwise than it is. The second use is that, by the service of this work, in the space of a short time you will teach a man ignorant of the Latin language, provided only that he knows how to read and write letters in his mother tongue, to write in the Latin language as you wish, ornamentedly or elegantly, and to conceal and hide all the secret mysteries of his will, and to announce them safely, secretly, and without suspicion to anyone he pleases who knows the art, as widely as he wishes. Again I warn you beforehand not to understand us as having promised otherwise than we promise. The third use, however, is that in a few hours you will teach one unskilled in the Roman tongue what is promised, [unclear].

[what we promise]: to write and read, but also to understand, if you prudently apply the duty of the office, which we have judged should be disclosed, not without reasonable cause. For the pupil of the new art will write a language that he did not know, and will understand and interpret Latin speech composed under regulated instruction, if you yourself have sufficiently directed him word for word. Finally, this instruction can be extended to all the things and affairs of the world. If anyone wishes to learn from me how these things can be done, let him remember first of all to show himself such that he deserves to receive it. For not everything is owed to everyone, but one person is to be preferred to another.

The fourth usefulness is that, through an enlargement of the likeness of the thing received, all these things can be extended into any language whatever, once the instructing binary has been reduced to unity. Yet not just anyone at all can do this everywhere, but only the man whom art and nature have dignified, with God going before him by his special grace.

The fifth usefulness is that, by imitation of likeness, we can communicate to one who knows the art of our invention whatever secrets of our mind we wish, abundantly, in many ways, and most widely, by various methods that cannot be known or noticed by anyone else. Here there is given a manifold speech without voice, through which, safely, securely, most widely, and with all suspicion removed, we shall be able to indicate most fully to those who know the art all the conceptions of our mind, however difficult they may be. And this marvelous invention has innumerable progressions, capable of all mysteries.

The sixth usefulness is that, through understanding this work, you will be able to discover any regulated metathesis or transposition of letters, and nevertheless to form them in such a way that they serve only those who know the art, and absolutely no one else in the world. And great is the force of metathesis in form and also in operation; it has many modes and is varied in many ways.

The seventh usefulness is that, through understanding this volume, a very great faculty is given to those who desire to enlarge the memory without labor, whenever the seeds of minutiae are set in their proper degrees. All things, for the sake of goodness, lie hidden wrapped in the secrets of words and figures. If anyone wishes to understand them more fully, let him call to mind that relentless labor conquers all things. For it will be enough for me to have discovered the principles of the art,

*** ij

and to have handed down a rough method of writing, and one deliberately unformed. For there was neither time nor reason for our inventions to be shaped in more polished form, lest honey produce vomiting in those who are nauseated, or truth produce hatred in those who are indignant. Every age must be valued according to its own merits, and swine are not to be adorned with pearls, nor burdened with precious gems. All things are untimely that do not agree with the customs and times of the mortals upon whom they are imposed.

There have been many very noble human talents in unsuitable times, and many new things are found almost daily in times not their own. What benefit did the marvelous invention of nautical art bring to the distinguished versifier Bartholus under Pope Innocent VIII? In a certain little book he offered it for sale for one hundred thousand ducats, when neither the supreme pontiff himself, nor the Venetians, nor the Genoese, to whom he proposed that his matter be bought, deigned even to come to terms with him for a modest price. For he promised that by his art he could keep a ship unharmed in the middle of the sea for thirty months, repair one that was broken, and bring back without danger whatever had been thrown into the depths. But no one cared. Nor does it escape me that many, with Naso, have perished by their own talent. It is therefore better to set a limit to knowledge than to expose oneself fruitlessly to the hatred and detraction of many, for whom it is more familiar to despise any knowledge than to have learned it.

END OF THE PREFACE

On the seventh day of April, in the year of the Lord’s nativity 1508.

THE KEY OF THE POLYGRAPHY OF JOHANNES TRITHEMIUS, ABBOT OF ST. JAMES AT WURZBURG, FORMERLY OF SPONHEIM, OF THE ORDER OF SAINT BENEDICT, OF THE OBSERVANCE OF THE FATHERS OF BURSFELDE.

[unclear]

PREFACE TO THE EXPLANATION OF THE WHOLE WORK OF THE POLYGRAPHY OF JOHANNES TRITHEMIUS, ABBOT OF PEAPOLIS, THAT IS, WURZBURG, AT ST. JAMES.

No one who reads these things, as I trust, will judge me either proud or superfluous because I myself have commented on the Polygraphy recently composed by me, especially if he has been able to weigh exactly what reason induced us to speak obscurely. For whatever, if made public, can do harm had reasonably to be concealed in mystical speech. The subject that we treat in the Polygraphy is, for the benefit of the commonwealth among good men, very good, useful, and honorable. For this reason, persuaded by a rational cause, we wrote it, so that by its service we might make good men safe and secure from the investigation of the wicked when they communicate their secrets to one another. But lest an opportunity be given to the wicked and perverse, who very often misuse even good inventions, to deceive the simpler and those less cautious in judging matters, we handed down in it mystical, that is, hidden, methods of writing, and covered the truth lying hidden in the kernel with certain coverings of figures. Yet we do not in the least doubt that any industrious man, eager for these matters, will easily grasp everything if he applies even moderate persistence in searching it out. For the things I have handed down are not so difficult, nor wrapped in such great mysteries, that they cannot be fully penetrated by a studious man. Thus everywhere we have tempered the riddles of our words, so that they are easily accessible to learned and studious men, and nevertheless remain inaccessible to sluggish dwellers in darkness. But after it pleased me to offer the work of Polygraphy itself,

dedicated, to the most serene and most unconquered Caesar of the Romans, Maximilian, ever august Emperor of the world, I judged that it would be worthwhile to make it clear and open with brief and few interpretations, lest the mind of his sacred majesty, which is daily stretched by many affairs and cares, be drawn back from understanding it by the obscurity of the mysteries. For, unless my opinion deceives me, the work will be the more pleasing and useful to his majesty, the shorter and clearer it is. First, therefore, with the Lord’s aid, we shall briefly explain the meaning of our purpose, which is contained in the prologue wrapped in various enigmas; then, book by book through the Polygraphy, we shall concisely unfold, to the strength of our ability, the methods of working, rules, cautions, and distinctions, in order, that remain necessary. All these things, so that they may more quickly become accessible to those who desire to know them, we shall show one after another through examples, and we shall be as brief as the cause and reason permit.

THE KEY OF THE EXPLANATION OF THE POLYGRAPHY OF JOHANNES TRITHEMIUS, ABBOT OF PEAPOLIS.

Exposition on the Prologue.

Our whole intention in the entire work of the Polygraphy is concerned with this proposition: that we should hand down fixed methods of writing secretly, by which kings and princes, nobles and commoners, priests and laymen, learned and unlearned alike, may secretly, safely, and without any suspicion of a hidden secret, communicate to one another and to any friends, even those far distant from one another, by the service of letters, whatever conception of their minds they need to communicate, and as often as there is need. And lest we seem to have presumed to do this either first or alone

we warn the reader that many of the ancients long ago, especially tyrants, princes, and kings, moved by a similar consideration, devised for themselves familiar and varied methods and rules of writing. By these they themselves attempted in particular what we have promised universally in our Polygraphy. From their number, for the sake of the example proposed, we have first introduced Caesar Augustus, whose secret method of writing you may understand plainly in this way.

He changed the breathings of the conceived voice from clear signs into obscure ones, and by a certain beautiful invention, by a movement of metathesis, made their barbarousness, resistant to wishes, obedient to his command. That is, the great Caesar Augustus, so that he might write secretly and safely whatever he wished, changed the letters of the alphabet by various transpositions, so that he put B for A, C for B, and so on with each letter in turn. And so that the writing, being more twisted, might remain more secret, he transposed the letters at his own discretion, breadthwise and lengthwise, to any distance of order, number, and place.

Mystery. And this receptive order, as though perpetual, subject to the will and to the reckoning of time, although it keeps messengers safe on the road from the attack of spies, nevertheless, since it has no regulated limits, makes all who encounter it anxious with suspicion of a hidden matter.

Explanation. Although no one can easily grasp with the understanding the secret mystery lying hidden beneath the transposition of letters, nevertheless this writing makes those into whose hands it comes suspicious of the hiding place of the matter enclosed within.

Mystery. Archimedes, that Syracusan, easily the foremost of mathematicians, his white bird, suited to his principles, naked through head and feet, and so forth.

Explanation. Archimedes had two little rods of the same length and thickness fashioned, either round or square. He kept one for himself and delivered the other to his absent friend. And whenever one wished to write something more secret to the other, he wound the white bird, that is, a sheet of papyrus of small width but of twice the length of the rod, around the wood, and fastened it with wax above and below. He then wrote on the sheet, which had been continuously and artfully joined to itself at the sides in a heap, whatever he wished. Then he loosened the sheet from the rod, and at once so great a distance appeared between the letters that not even a single word cohered with another. He turned the sheet

and, when he wished, wrote in the same way on the other side. Nor was there anyone ignorant of this practice who could have tracked down the secret. But the one who had the other rod, when he had received the sheet, fastened it on and restored the letters to their former order.

Mystery. Marcus T. Cicero, the eloquent orator of the Romans, using talent and art, changed the small elements of speech into signs, and the rest.

Explanation. He wrote a book of shorthand signs for his son, which the blessed martyr Cyprian later enlarged for the use of Christians: that is, in the manner of a dictionary, where first the characters or signs are placed in order, and afterward the words designated by those same characters, so that any given word is signified by the sign placed before it. We once saw, written in these signs or characters, a complete and beautifully copied Latin psalter in the library of the greater church of Strasbourg. Some man, ignorant of judgment in such matters, had placed on its outside the following title: Psalter in the Armenian language. But he was wrong, since it should rather have been written thus: Latin psalter written in Tullian characters. For each character represents one Latin word.

Nor am I mistaken in this judgment, since I possess the very dictionary of Cicero, corrected by Saint Cyprian, written complete and uncorrupted in an ancient volume, which I have seen nowhere else. So great is the abundance of signs or characters, with the words subject to them, that they are altogether sufficient for writing in the Latin language whatever you wish.

Mystery. Faramund, the forty-third from Marcomer king of the Franks, when in the year of the Lord’s nativity 424 he powerfully entered the borders of the Gauls, and the rest.

Explanation. From the time when the kings of the Franks, having gone out with their people from the Scythian borders in the year 430 before the nativity of Christ, settled at the mouths of the Rhine, where Guelders now is, they waged continual war with the Gauls for almost nine hundred years, and at last violently made them subject to themselves, as we have written in the first volume of our Annals. From these, the aforesaid King Faramund, so that he might send messengers safely through the kingdom, devised new letters of his own, which no one could know without his voluntary instruction. Nor did he use only one new alphabet, nor a few, but many.

Mystery. Clodius Crinitus, son of Faramund, and after him king of the Franks,

...of them, who subjected all Gaul to himself and, after destroying the Romans whom he found there, used his father’s inventions in secret writings. Explanation. This king devised alphabets of his own and new ones, and gave one to each of his commanders, while he alone kept knowledge of them all in his own possession. Mystery. Charles, called the Great, the sixty-third king of the Franks, who was the first of the Franks to wear the diadem of the Roman empire, and the rest. Explanation. This man, the elder son of King Pippin, is read to have been born as duke of Brabant in the county of Namur, bordering on the people of Liège, although some assert that he was born in the village of Ingelheim, not far from Mainz. He too invented various methods of writing, and, with Nanno the grammarian lending his assistance, devised different alphabets, by which he communicated secrets to the prefects of the kingdom in a special manner. Mystery. The Northmen, who once came out from the borders of Gothia, when they were laying waste Gaul in a cruel invasion, called owls from Greece and prepared a safe hiding-place for their secrets, and the rest. Explanation. The Northmen, while ranging through Gaul, as the monk Bede in England bears witness, in order to write their secrets safely among themselves, substituted Greek numerals for Latin letters, from A as the first as far as the twenty-fourth point, W, or gu, according to the custom of the Gauls. This manner of writing is altogether very beautiful: in it all the letters are Greek, and according to the order of Pelasgian numbering they designate our Latin letters, as A, 1; B, 2; C, 3; D, 4; E, 5; F, 6; G, 7; and so consequently as far as W, which is 24. Neither a Greek nor a Latin will understand this writing unless he has first learned the method and art of the device. Mystery. Our Bede, a monk in England, not ignorant of the deed of the Northmen, described many ancient inventions similar to these, by which they made a path bright in mysteries into one that was dark. He himself set down artrology, and the rest. Explanation. This monk Bede, in his little book On the Inventions of the Ancients, reviewed many and various methods of writing and marking secretly, by which they safely announced their secrets to friends and spoke without voice to those present. He was the first of all to commend artrology and dactylogy to letters; by their use one man most securely discloses to another whatever secret he wishes, which no one else among the bystanders will notice, much less understand.

He taught that this same thing can be done in many other ways as well; since we have written nothing about them in the Polygraphy, we rightly decline to say more here. We long ago assigned the place proper to these difficult matters in the Steganography, which we do not yet intend to publish. And who could set out all the ancient methods of writing secretly? For some had as familiar servants in the practice of the art certain owls called Philophoti; others had Mysophoti; others called both into practice from the art. Again, some transposed the known letters of the common alphabet; others fashioned characters of their own for themselves under the guise of barbarian letters. Again, likewise, some used the service of visible letters, writing with cinnabar or common ink; others, however, formed invisible characters at will according to their purpose. The methods of visible characters for secret writing are exceedingly many and altogether innumerable; to mention all of them is neither our wish nor within our power. Of invisible characters there are three kinds more commonly used among mortals today. The first is called dermatic, by which a certain artificial writing is made on the backs of messengers, visible only through washing with a certain liquid. [unclear] The third kind is called alleotic, which is multiple and varied, both in form and in matter, and has almost innumerable methods of writing secretly. Its writing is made on paper or without paper, with nemilua and cala, with raphocam, lapolce, and various other things. Letters are likewise written in various ways and hidden in places: under race tabulata, under rosi rilacubior, in leopi, in necostas, in ceocali, locubat, in ratera, in lispilia, and in other nearly infinite things of the same sort. But since none of these things serves our present purpose on this occasion, we should therefore hasten to the things that the plan requires. There is also another kind, dactiletron, not indeed of writing, but of signs, by which one person can communicate the conception of his mind to another in very subtle ways. This too is varied by so many differences that there is no one in the world who could enumerate all the species of so great a mystery. In the principal mode, at the same time

By the principal and at the same time manual method, and by many others artificially derived from it, while sitting at a table or in any other place, you will be able to communicate whatever you wish to one who knows the art, very safely and without anyone’s suspicion. Finally, that you may disclose the secret of your mind without letters to someone absent, even when the very person who performs the office of messenger does not know it, remains written among the inventions of steganography.

Indeed, since kings and princes encounter many affairs of which they sometimes do not trust themselves to give knowledge safely enough to their vicars far away by ordinary letters, it would be worthwhile for each of them to have some special methods of writing and announcing, by which they might most safely make known their secrets to friends, especially in these times, when, with license to sin prevailing, trustworthy faith is found nowhere in the world. The messengers of princes are everywhere captured by savage robbers, stripped, beaten, and very often killed; nor do the impious plunderers spare even the letters of kings sealed and closed with rings. Hence it would be necessary for your commonwealth, O most glorious Caesar Maximilian, that you put on the skin of Hercules, brandish the club in your hands, and purge the world committed to you by God of these savage monsters. There will never be peace in the kingdom unless the bacucei are removed from the midst. Whoever disturbs the peace of the kingdom shows himself to be the king’s enemy. These are the robbers who beset the roads of travelers and seize what belongs to others; with them the earth is full today, and nowhere is the road safe for those who walk.

A BRIEF EXPLANATION OF THOSE THINGS WHICH SEEM RATHER OBSCURE IN THE FIRST BOOK OF THE POLYGRAPHIA.

Although nothing obscure is contained in the first book of the Polygraphia, nevertheless, lest its composition perhaps seem deep to simpler readers, we briefly explain the things that are thought more difficult. We have arranged in sequence more than nine thousand words of the Latin language under almost four hundred alphabets, in such a way that if from each alphabet only one word after another is taken from beginning to end, they cohere with one another and form a suitable Latin discourse.

For it will be a very convenient method of writing most secretly whatever we wish, since each word represents the letter set before it at its head. Nor should it trouble you, reader, that the multitude of words in the open text contains a brief meaning in the hidden one, since within this childish arrangement of ours there lies concealed a higher method of writing, more broadly and far more secretly, whatever you wish; public reason has forbidden us to make it plain to everyone. But whoever is endowed with talent and applies the necessary powers to investigation will find subtler things among the teachings hidden here, and, to his wonder, will clearly understand things previously unknown. Nevertheless, this open method of writing will suffice for everything, since you can repeat it as many times as you wish, and the repeated narration will always vary.

For if, as we have said, you take one word from the first alphabet, one also from the second, and so consequently one from each, and one from those interposed outside the ordered line, up to the period or the end of the book, a Latin and sufficiently suitable discourse will arise for you. But care must be taken that at one time, all at once, no more than one word be taken from a single alphabet, and that the writer, through negligence or excessive haste, not skip over some alphabet and confuse the order of the narration.

By “day” understand the open narration; by “night,” however, the latent and hidden one, which should not be too long but brief. The examples that follow in the text concerning the invisible soul and the body that is seen pertain to both narrations, the hidden and the manifest. “As often as the leaf is moved by the wind,” and the rest: we advise that you count the secret narration in relation to the open one in such a way that both end together at the close of any period. But if anything remains over from the secret matter, let it be lengthened with such moderation that both narrations end at one point, lest confusion from an eclipse be produced.

The other things that follow in the first Polygraphic explanation are also implicitly referred to all the things we have said. It should be noted, however, that there is no word vacant under the order of the alphabets, but each represents the letter set before it at its head. So that the reader may not lack perfect knowledge of this matter, let us explain it by an example. Let us suppose a case: that a wicked man asks through you to be promoted with some friend of yours, but you, in order to cut off his importunate requests and yet not promote an unworthy man

A very suitable method for writing with the utmost secrecy whatever we wish, in which each word represents the letter set before it at its head. Nor should it trouble you, reader, that a multitude of words in the open text contains a brief meaning in the hidden text, since within this childish arrangement of ours there lies another method of writing whatever you wish much more broadly and much more secretly, which public reason has forbidden us to make available to all. But anyone endowed with intelligence, or who applies the necessary things to the investigation, will find subtler teachings hidden in these matters and will clearly understand things wonderfully unknown before.

Nevertheless, this open method of writing will suffice for everything, since you can repeat it as often as you wish, and the repeated narrative will always be varied. For if, as we have said, you take one word from the first alphabet, one also from the second, and so consequently one from each, and one from those inserted outside the ordered line, up to a period or the end of the book, a Latin and sufficiently coherent discourse will arise for you. But care must be taken that at one time, and all at once, no more than one word is taken from one alphabet, and that the writer, through negligence or excessive falsification, does not pass over any alphabet and confuse the order of the narrative.

By day understand the open narrative; by night, however, the hidden and concealed one, which should not be too long but brief. Those things that follow in the paradigmatic text concerning the invisible soul and the body that is seen pertain to both narratives, the hidden and the manifest. As often as a leaf is moved by the wind, and so on, we advise you to count the secret narrative in relation to the open one, so that both may end together at the foot of each period. But if anything of the secret matter remains over, let it be enlarged by such moderation that both narratives end at one point, lest confusion or an omission be produced from them. The other things that follow in the first Polygraphy are referred implicitly both to the explanatory instruction and to everything we have said.

It should be noted, however, that no word under the order of the alphabets is vacant; rather, each one represents the letter set before it at its head. So that the reader may not lack perfect knowledge of this matter, we shall clarify the sentence by an example. Let us suppose the case that a wicked man asks through you to be promoted with some friend of his. But you, so as to cut off the importunate requests and yet not promote an unworthy man, may write more secretly to the friend through the very man who is making the request, so that he does not understand: Beware of that man, because he is a thief and a very worthless scoundrel.

we frequently need in our German language. For anyone who is ignorant of the Latin tongue may write his hidden secret in German beneath a Latin discourse without any difficulty.

NOW FOLLOW THE RULES or cautions to be observed in the operation of this book.

I. The first rule or caution advises you that you should write down, as carefully as you can, on a small sheet the secret of your mind that you wish to communicate to an absent friend who knows the art and has the book of Polygraphy, whether in the Latin language or in German, or in any other language you wish that can be expressed in Roman letters. Then place the sheet so written before you, so that for each single letter of the secret you may be able to fit a corresponding word. For, as we have shown in this practice of writing, a whole word is taken. We gave an example a little earlier in what precedes.

II. The second caution instructs you, as has been said, not to take more than one word at a time from any alphabet in a single narrative of public Latin speech; otherwise you would both confuse the open meaning and wholly draw away the friend to whom you had written from understanding the mystery.

III. Third, one must take the greatest care not to skip over any alphabet through negligence without taking from it one word suited to the secret. Likewise one must provide that, whenever one or more words occur outside the sequence of the alphabet, you take either the whole upper line or the lower one, and not both.

IIII. Fourth, care must be taken that whenever the discourse of the open speech has been brought to a complete sentence, the next sentence should take its beginning from a larger, thickened letter, according to the form of the preceding example, in which, according to the sense of the Latin discourse, we have taken large letters at the beginning and small letters in the rest, in the common manner. When the secret of your mind is lengthy, so that it exceeds the narrative of the open speech, if much remains, begin again from the beginning; if little remains, let the discourse be recalled at will from any place whatever.
