For no one even moderately skilled in this technique will be unable to know where you have begun again. Nor is there any need to fear the consonance of the speech—

consonance, for whenever one begins from the start, a new form of discourse will always follow, with the open narrative varying along with the hidden one. The continuation can also be made from the end of the first book through the second.

V. Fifth, we advise that whenever you wish to write by this art about a difficult matter, you prepare for yourself a small booklet, in which you write your secret mystery in open discourse. Whoever sees or reads this booklet will not think that any secret lies hidden there; and even if he has a suspicion, he will not be able to discover anything of what you are writing.

VI. Sixth, it should be noted that if you transpose the order of the words throughout the whole Polygraphia, changing it by metathesis in each alphabet, and have two volumes written according to it, one for yourself and the other for any friend, you will write between yourselves, with the greatest security, whatever you wish; nor does anyone live on earth who could penetrate your secrets. This transposition, moreover, can be made in infinitely many ways.

VII. Seventh, we forewarn you that one must write polygraphically in one way to a person ignorant of the Latin language, and in another way to one skilled in it. For the former, all the words must be written out in full, without abbreviation, distinctly, completely, beautifully, and in every way legibly, without separation, without division, and without confusion, lest, deceived by an error, he think that one word is two, or judge that two are one. The things that are set down must be heeded.

VIII. Eighth, care must be taken that the person to whom you write mystically by this art possess a book like yours in every respect; otherwise you would write in vain and fruitlessly to someone who does not understand.

IX. Ninth, if you wish this technique to remain forever secret and hidden, rewrite the Polygraphia anew, but do not place the letters of the alphabet before the words, and no one will easily suspect the method of the secret. But so that no difficulty may arise for the writer and reader in the mystery, let the letters of the alphabet be written on a small slip in the order corresponding to the words, and let it be fitted, movable, to the headings of those words. The letters may also be engraved on a copper plate, so that they can be moved from one order to another.

X. Tenth, it should be known that although we do not use the Pythagorean Y in the words of German and Latin, we have nevertheless admitted it on account of the Greek language, so that we might have the twelvefold number doubled. Likewise we have taken the doubled W as the twenty-fourth letter, because it is wholly necessary for us in the German language.

XI. Eleventh, the person who receives letters written from the Polygraphia to be read should know that understanding is needed in reading. And therefore, whenever he receives a sheet or booklet written polygraphically, he should go to a secret place and, after opening the book of the Polygraphia which he must have with him, examine each word through all the alphabets, and very carefully note with chalk on a table, or with ink on paper, what letter each one represents. And when he has gone through the whole letter in this way, let him compose the letters into words, and he will easily understand what lay hidden in secret.

XII. Twelfth, let kings and princes take note, who have many deputies in different places, to all of whom it is not prudent to write with one single kind of hidden narrative. Therefore, so that they may have a proper secret method of writing to each one individually, let them change the order of the words as many times as they wish to have separate methods. Thus they themselves will possess the methods of writing of all of them, and no subject will understand the method of another. For the variable methods of writing more secretly by this art are infinite.

XIII. Thirteenth, it should be noted that, in order to stop the mouths of those speaking wicked things, we have shown the truth of this new invention of ours to be possible by placing the words in the alphabets of the first book so that they cohere with one another in such a way that, in the manner of an exhortation and supplication offered to God, they produce a fitting and Latin discourse. Under this narrative we can conceal whatever secrets occur to us, and write in such a way to a friend skilled in the art that if all the people in the whole world came together as one, they could never discover the secret lying hidden beneath the open discourse, provided it has been arranged correctly.

XIIII. Fourteenth, it should be known that in this very invention of our Polygraphia there still lie hidden certain things far better than those written above: namely, how, in a few days, not to say hours, you will be able to instruct someone ignorant of the Latin language so that he knows how to write, read, and understand Latin, not indeed absolutely everything, but, in a fixed manner, whatever necessary matter may occur to him in his affairs on any subject whatever. Likewise, how you may safely, securely, and most secretly make known to your friend far away, who knows the technique of the art, all the conceptions of your mind without writings and with the messenger unaware, and sometimes even naturally without a messenger and without [unclear].

Without any superstition, danger, or fear. But reason has moved us to let these things remain buried in their own hiding places with the rest, since it neither pleases me nor is at all useful to cast precious stones to the wind, or to undertake difficult things without the fruit of gratitude. Finally, beneath these matters there lie no small mysteries of subtlety concerning medicines, herbs, plants, precious stones, rivers, the members of the human body, brute animals, saints, nations, cosmography, astronomy and the seven liberal arts, and also concerning all those things that are in human use, and concerning the universal world, both of visible and invisible things. And, lest we be more prolix than is right, all things that exist in the world, through an amplification of the likeness of the art of polygraphy shown above, serve a mystical teaching.

XV. Fifteenth, note that all these things that we have handed down as discoveries in the Polygraphy are certain small introductions in comparison with those things that still remain to be discovered and written in this same faculty. We pass over these in silence, lest we seem to boast in vain. For we have given to minds fit for invention an occasion for discovering greater things than we have either written or perhaps been able to discover. Let him who can add, for the completion of this invention, those things that he knows to be useful; but he who cannot should not rashly judge what he does not understand.

An explanation of those things which seemed more obscure in the second book of the Polygraphy.

In the second book of the Polygraphy, apart from the order and sequence of the words, nothing new is first handed down; and therefore one and the same method of working will apply in both books, and all the things that we said were to be observed in the first, we admonish must also be observed diligently in the second. In the narration alone a difference of discourse is clearly seen to have arisen, since the former is composed concerning our Lord, the Son of God, while this one is raised to his mother, the ever-untouched Virgin. Now in the second book there are three hundred and eight alphabets placed before the words in order, yet under different subjects. For from the beginning the narration of the discourse is directed to our Lady herself; afterward the Lord's Prayer is enlarged under twenty-four alphabets; then seij

be distinguished, lest the person to whom you write take two for one, or one for two, because that would give birth to a great error. Let us set down an example of this matter.

Abrin madon badis, cadulur pasu, adin loroff masara damis, boda omo dro mi drus uares mastron pha lares medas rassut madebor tara, mesen baiu phosat, galos, prosol fane lemoros, arosocabil neso, hamol heliet rhamil fesia doron hubor rodex.

In this narration of fictive speech is contained this brief secret sentence of a friend warning a friend of danger: "Do not come to court, because the king is angry with you." You see how easy, safe, and secure this method is for writing and announcing to a friend who understands it whatever you wish. In all cases, however, you should know that care must be taken, as was said before, not to take more than one word from any alphabet. Whenever you have brought the narration of the invented speech to the end of the book, while the secret of your mind has not yet been completed, begin again from the beginning, and do this as often as necessary. Nevertheless, each person will be able, at his own discretion, to change these words of ours, improve them, and add more, provided that he avoids a consonance that breaks out disgracefully in the sounds.

Explanation of the fourth book of our Polygraphy.

In the fourth book of the Polygraphy, by a similar method, we have placed words invented by us under alphabetical order, but in one thing alone we deliberately differ from the preceding book. For in the preceding book the words contain in themselves no property other than that they represent the letters placed before them at the head. But in the fourth book, which we now have in hand, each word contains its own meaning, and nevertheless also designates the letters placed before it. They have within what they display without, because the second letter of each word always serves the hidden mystery, as we shall make clear in the following example.

Ecorach hanasar dulay semalas, chorion suriel anephor schabaras husarat uiimalo tropon tumelech amasar.

For the understanding of this mystery, from each [unclear]

from each word take only the second letter, and you will find this meaning hidden: “Beware this man.” For the second letter in Ecorach is C, in hanafar A, in dulay V, in semalas E; join these four letters and they will make this word: “Beware.” And so one should proceed through the remaining words as far as the end of the book; and if any hidden mystery still remains to be written, one must return to the beginning as often as necessary, until the secret has been completed in full. In this most secret manner of writing, if anyone has been trained by long practice, he does not need the book, but will easily compose, on the spot, words suited to his purpose. But anyone less practiced in composition necessarily requires access to the book from which he is to write. For the reader, a copy of the volume will not be necessary, since without the book he can easily find the hidden secret by means of the second letters everywhere. Yet in great, difficult, or dangerous matters this method of writing should not be trusted as sufficiently safe, because the industry of a skilled man might by chance discover the hidden mystery. This method of writing, however, can also be changed by an intelligent man, so that the significant letters are placed in the third or fourth position of the word, with the words altered.

A Brief Explanation of the Fifth Book of Our Polygraphia.

In the fifth book of the Polygraphia we have handed down various methods of writing secretly through the transposition of common letters, arranged in such an order that under their covering we shall be able to write and announce everything safely to an absent friend. The progress of the transposition of letters is, to speak in our own manner, almost infinite, since from one alphabet innumerable alphabets arise by metathesis. First we described a straight table containing twenty-four alphabets; by understanding it, as many alphabets can be composed as there are stars counted in the firmament of heaven. For as many letters as there are in that table, so many times do ten hundred thousand arise by art, according to the order of the alphabet. After this we set out a reversed table, which changes into another as often as you change the first letter at the head. The letter in the first, straight table is B, and in the reversed one Z. Into the fourth place, as often as [unclear]

he wishes, he may devise for himself more beautiful characters. All the synthemata of this book are sufficiently open and clear, and therefore they need no explanation, even a brief one. Yet those things which stand as newly invented by us require a definite declaration, lest perhaps they be judged to have been set down without reason. First of all, we have made all the letters of the Latins numerical, after the manner of the Hebrews and Greeks, thinking it shameful for us if we should be found inferior to them in this respect. For what does it matter that we have doubled certain letters so that they might suffice for an infinite number, since the Jews, compelled by the same necessity, did that very thing long ago? And the Greeks, because of a lack of letters, admitted certain signs into the number, since they could not double the letters. But we, because we are pressed by an equal lack of letters, have admitted two signs: namely this one, &, which our scribes use for et; nor does it matter whether it is written thus, &, or thus, et, provided that it represents six in number. We have added another, 9, which our scribes write in abbreviation for con and com indifferently; here, in the order of numbers, it represents six hundred. By the same necessity we have doubled two letters, namely r, z, and s: the straight r signifies ninety, the curved z one hundred, the long s two hundred, and the closed s three hundred. Further, the doubled w, which we have placed in the order of the alphabet because of the character of the German language, represents the final letter, and in the series of numbers one thousand. Let us set down a tabular example of this new invention of ours for the system of numbers, so that whoever wishes to know the method may have a definite guide before his eyes. For what has always been easy for the Hebrews and the Greeks will not be impossible for us. The table of numbers follows.

We have shown a sufficient method of numbering by Latin letters, after the manner of the Hebrews and Greeks. We have reasonably placed it here by way of digression, although it is also found earlier in the sixth book. And by the fact that, as we proceed, we have here enclosed our number within thirty times one hundred thousand, we openly declare that it can be extended to infinity. If this method of numbers displeases anyone, he will easily be able to devise a better one.

Also, in imitation of the Northmen, from the numerical letters written above we have arranged a new alphabet, by which you will be able safely to write and report to an absent friend whatever secret you wish. This method of writing is so secret, as well as new and never before us seen or heard of, that it seems to me wholly impossible that it could be understood by anyone without the service of a teacher. But now let us set down its alphabet.

a a.1 f g 7 ic n 13 ih t 19 b b.2 g h 8 id o 14 k u 20 c c.3 h i 9 ie p 15 ka x 21 d d.4 i k 10 i et q 16 kb y 22 e e 5 ia l 11 if r 17 kc z 23 f f 6 ib m 12 ig s 18 kd w 24

Behold, then: you now have here an alphabet made from the Roman numerical letters in imitation of the Northmen. With it you will be able most safely to write and report to an absent friend whatever you wish, and no hidden observer will be able to penetrate your secret, except the one who knows the secret of the art. For all who see the writing will think that the letters have been transposed, and they will labor in vain in reckoning them. Let us set down an example.

Iaaihid ifeib, iefiegeicehfib. oa' eihid. i et Fahb. gidibid. eigh. ietigigh ib ig. & if. iaaihifid, ihe icda'ia. eih. icie&'iaib.

The hidden meaning of this writing is as follows: Beware the bearer of the present letters, because he is a very wicked man, a thief, a robber, a liar, and worthless. By this demonstration of an example it is easily given to be understood how safe and secret this method of writing is universally, in every language known to the writer,

and in every cause or business, however arduous, secret, great, or lengthy. Nor do I think there is a man living in the world who, from his own ingenuity and without a teacher, could read this very writing. For all who see it will think it nothing other than that the letters have been transposed; and when they cannot obtain an understanding of them, at last, wearied by despair, they will cease from their investigation, and whatever you have written will remain hidden. For no one, as I think, will examine by his own powers this art of writing secretly as it is, unless he has either the Polygraphy, or this key to it, at hand, or has been instructed by another.

From these numerical letters many other alphabets can also be given according to the order of numbering, when the beginning for writing alphabetically is taken not from unity but from any other following number. But in that progression you should know that one must take care that no more than two numerable characters be taken to represent one letter. Therefore, when you have arrived at wowo, that is, ten times one hundred thousand, stop your course and do not wander further, lest the multitude of characters confuse the beauty of writing by corrupting it. For after unity is excluded, ten times one hundred thousand, with the characters included, are sufficient for almost thirty individual alphabets. Yet the method of the first alphabet, beginning with unity, is better for enveloping written secrets in proportion as it is shorter and simpler. Finally, it renders the writing less tortuous.

We have also arranged another alphabet, with the Latin letters distributed in a flowing order and transposed without a rule; in imitation of it others too can be made almost without number. Its likeness is now set down.

o a t g c n 9 t p b h a o k u q c i h p n x r d w y q m y i e l d r z s f z m g s f w

c ij

Let us also set down an example of this alphabet, to prove that a secret can lie hidden in it:

Quogozozugi, yfarz din, uc, qdcquxua, rigidiuosi, aqquirix tz, fti, idra, yfocsaqufg, uc, coddotacuoz, ofogui, iuvg, ci, hidioz.

This writing contains in itself the following meaning: “Know, my friend, that the king has decreed in council that you are to be killed. Therefore flee as quickly as possible into Narragonia, away from his presence, lest you perish.” This too is a tortuous mode of writing and is subject to no regular rule, since at the writer’s pleasure it can be varied and changed by chance transposition as much as anyone wishes.

Next it should be noted that at the end of the sixth book of the Polygraphia we handed down another way of writing by numerical signs, which people commonly call ciphers. Under its covering you will safely write to an absent friend whatever you wish, and no one unskilled in the art will be able either to discover or to suspect that a secret lies hidden, especially if the rules we gave concerning these matters are observed with careful diligence. This is that the paper should be formed in the manner of an astronomical table, as though it contained something pertaining to the reckoning of the stars: namely, so that characters of the signs or planets are inserted, in order that anyone into whose hands it may perhaps fall by chance, led on by the likeness of a table, will think that no secret lies hidden in it, but will suppose that everything pertains to some astronomical calculation.

We have arranged twelve alphabets according to the number of the twelve signs of the Zodiac, assigning to each one the number twenty-four in place of letters. The first of these, Aries, begins from one and ends at twenty-four. Yet we advise that in great and difficult matters one should avoid beginning from one, because this way of writing can easily be suspected on account of that very thing. But whoever wishes to use his natural industry prudently will discover subtler things from ours, and what we have handed down not fully polished he will easily make better.

In the numerical orchema great secrets lie hidden; if anyone properly understands it, he will penetrate many mysteries of numbers. For we had neither the time nor the reason on this occasion to pour everything out into public view, but in our judgment what we have done will have been enough for the instruction of those to whom our inventions will one day be pleasing, so that they may have many ways not only of secretly writing whatever they wish

to absent sharers in the art, but also one way of bringing forth many better and subtler ones, according to the capacity of each person’s understanding. Likewise, since the orchemata of numbers are sufficiently open and clear in their proper places, and their tables have also been set out, it was not necessary here to repeat what has already been said, lest excessive prolixity create weariness for the reader. Nor did I judge it necessary to set down an example of secret writing by means of numerical figures, since there is no difficulty in knowing the method for all who possess even moderate intelligence.

With similar ease the very ancient signs of reckoning that we have brought back into the light will be able to be understood and grasped; by them the knowledge of numbers is extended to infinity. For whenever a small stroke is placed above a smaller number, a thousandfold value is indicated. Thus x with a stroke above it means ten thousand; C, one hundred thousand; M, a thousand thousand; X, ten thousand thousand; .M., a thousand thousand thousand; and so consequently as far as you may wish to proceed in numbering, without limit.

THE END OF THE KEY TO THE POLYGRAPHIA of Johannes Trithemius, abbot of Peapoli, to Emperor Maximilian.

END OF THE POLYGRAPHY Moreover in a certain manuscript of M. Jacob Moreover

APOLOGY OF JOHANNES TRITHEMIUS, prefixed to the Steganography.

It is the opinion of many that the ancient philosophers and sages of art and nature, if they had discovered any secrets, concealed them by various methods and figures, lest they come to the knowledge of wicked men. The more learned among the Jews also confirm that Moses, the most famous leader of the Israelite people, in his description of the creation of heaven and earth, covered the ineffable secrets of mysteries with simple words. Likewise Saint Jerome, most learned among our own, says that in the Apocalypse almost as many mysteries lie hidden as there are words. I pass over the sages of the Greeks, men of no small reputation and glory among their own people, who, devoting their labor to the writing of fables, handed down one thing to the unlearned and another to learned men in the course of a single narrative, by a prudent invention. These most devoted lovers of wisdom, even if I cannot perfectly imitate them because of the slowness of my intellect, I nevertheless judge it a beautiful and glorious thing to admire, and, with whatever diligence I can, to read and venerate. Thus, when I consider that they discovered great things beyond other men by their own study, I drive myself, doing a kind of violence to myself, toward some imitation of them, even if among the latest. Nor, as I think, has my opinion wholly deceived me, since by continuous zeal for reading I have both learned many things that I did not know before, and have reserved my thoughts for investigating more secret matters. For even if I am not of such great learning or industry that I would dare to profess that I have grasped that method of the ancient sages for concealing mysteries, nevertheless I have devised certain methods, not altogether to be despised, as it seems to me, of writing secretly and of concealing, entirely without any suspicion, whatever you wish. At the request of the most serene prince, lord Philip, Count Palatine of the Rhine and Duke of Bava-

ria, Prince Elector of the Roman Empire, most wise patron of philosophers, than whom no one has seemed to me more worthy for this great secret to be revealed to him, I have committed them to writing and reduced them into the following volume, not without great labor, lest this great secret come to the ears of common, ignorant, or wicked men. I ask you, reader, whoever you may be, to consider how many evils could be committed in the commonwealth by wicked and slippery people through this science, if it came to the knowledge of many: adulteries, fornications, conspiracies, betrayals, murders, robberies, and countless evils. For just as a good and honorable man can safely and without any suspicion from anyone disclose and express the secret of his will to another who knows this art, as often as he wishes, for private or common benefit, so any perverse, slippery, and malicious man will be able to communicate his evil desire without any suspicion, however shamefully, to persons agreeable to his pleasure, with every obstacle wholly removed. Nor could trust between married people remain safe thereafter, since a woman, though until now ignorant of the Latin language, made most learned through holy and modest words of any language or idiom, could understand very fully the evil and immodest will of her lover, even while her husband presents and praises the letters, and in the same way could most safely send back to him her own desire, at whatever length she wished, in sufficiently eloquent speech. Indeed, although this science may seem childish to some, nevertheless, if it were made public, the whole order of the commonwealth would be disturbed, public trust would perish, letters, instruments of writing, and finally all the very conversations of men would be turned into perpetual suspicion. No one would any longer trust letters, however good, honorable, and holy; no one would put faith in epistles, because, however holy and modest the words might be, deceit, fraud, and evil deception would nevertheless always be thought to lie beneath them. Men would become fearful in all things, and no less suspicious of mutual conversations than of any letters whatever. Nor will anyone ever be able to become so learned and expert in this science itself that there would not remain infinite methods, sufficient for all purposes, of writing secretly and most hiddenly, which he himself has not yet grasped. For this science is a chao

chaos of infinite magnitude, which no one can comprehend. For however learned you may be in this art, what you understand is still less than what you do not know. For it is a property of this science always to make the pupil, provided he is diligent and willing, incomparably more learned than the master.

THERE FOLLOWS THE EXPOSITION OF THE MOST ILLUSTRIOUS MAN ADOLPH GLAVBRG, PATRICIAN OF FRANKFURT, with examples of those things that were either passed over by the author or treated less clearly.

The great Roman emperor was one of these.) On this method of writing, see Suetonius Tranquillus in the Life of Augustus, chapter 88, and in the Life of Julius Caesar, chapter 80. “There are also extant,” he says, “letters to Cicero, and likewise to his intimates, on domestic matters, in which, if anything had to be conveyed more secretly, he wrote it in signs, that is, with the order of the letters so arranged that no word could be formed. If anyone wished to investigate them, he should substitute the fourth letter of the alphabet, that is, d, for a, and exchange the remaining letters in the same way.” Moreover Isidore also mentions a letter of Augustus to his son, in which he writes thus: “Since innumerable things constantly arise which we must write to one another and keep secret, let us have signs between ourselves, if you wish, such that when something must be written by us, we write the following letter in place of each single letter, in this way: b for a, c for b, and thereafter the others by the same method. But for the letter z one must return to double aa.”

Archimedes of Syracuse.) Similar to this is what is read in Gellius, book 17, chapter 9. The ancient Lacedaemonians, when they wished to disguise and conceal letters sent officially to their commanders, lest, if they were intercepted by enemies, their plans should become known, used to send letters made in the following kind. There were two round sticks, somewhat oblong, of equal thickness and the same length, shaved and finished in like fashion. One was given to the commander setting out for war; the other the magistrates kept at home under oath and seal. When there was need of more secret letters, they wound around the stick a long strip of leather of moderate thinness, or as much as the matter required, in a round and simple coil, so that the edges of the joined and adhering strip that was being folded met on every side. Then they wrote letters on that strip across the transverse edges of the joins, in lines running from top to bottom. When the strip had been written on in this way, they unrolled it from the stick and sent it to the commander, who knew the device. The unrolling of the strip made the letters broken and mutilated, and scattered their parts and strokes into widely separated places. Therefore, if that strip fell into the hands of enemies, they could conjecture nothing at all from it. But when the man to whom it had been sent received it, he took the matching stick that he had, wrapped the strip around it to the end just as he knew it had to be done, and so the letters, coming together again around the same circumference of the stick, once more joined up and presented a complete and uncorrupted letter, easy to read. The Lacedaemonians call this kind of letter a scytale. See also Plutarch in the Life of Lysander.

There is also another no less ingenious method of concealing letters, described by Jerome Cardano in his books On Subtleties. Take two equal sheets of parchment ruled for writing, and in the very lines make small holes scattered here and there in corresponding positions on both sheets, yet according to the size or height of the letters. Some will contain seven letters, some three, some eight or ten, so that all the holes together contain one hundred and twenty letters, when joined with all the letters that can be written in them. But when there is need, write your first sentence as briefly as you can, so that the number of letters—

...that the sentence contain a smaller number of letters than the one which the intervals can take. Then, with the membrane placed underneath the holes, you will write that sentence, and likewise on another and another; finally fill the spaces of the first membrane, completing and deleting sentences until the sense is coherent. You will complete this second sentence on the second membrane, so that the words and sentences seem to cohere; on the third also you will fit it in such a way that, with the first letters left unharmed, the whole sentence, the number and size of the words, stand firm and retain a certain neatness. When these things have been done, place the pattern which you have cut over an equal membrane, and at the edges of the holes mark very fine points as far as the letters which you wish to write extend. Then take the third membrane, and write the letter with continuous words, in a proper order of spaces and also of the size of the letters, so that the first sentence and its words are contained within the boundaries of the points. Thus no suspicion of fraud then remains; the other person, when he receives it and places the pattern over it, at once understands the thought of your mind. Nor, although the labor is not light, can anything equal to this be found for communicating one's intention to friends in dangerous times.

Marcus Tullius.) The opinion is that Cicero devised single and special characters for individual Latin words, with which, if necessity demanded, he wrote a speech, however long, both with very few signs and in the greatest secrecy. And in this way, they report, the speech of Cato, that the conspirators should be put to death, was preserved and committed to writing, when Cicero, as consul, appointed very swift writers to record speeches with notes of this kind. That the ancients also followed a certain similar method for writing words quickly and compendiously, so that they often signified a word by a single letter, is attested by Valerius Probus, Petrus Crinitus, Angelus Decembrius, and also the very ancient monuments collected with the greatest diligence by Petrus Appianus and Bartholomaeus Amantius. But this technique of writing will be treated more carefully below.

Our Bede in England.) On computation and the language of the fingers

d iij

I find these things in Bede, On the Reckoning of Times. When you say one, bending the little finger on the left hand, you will set it against the middle joint of the palm. When you say two, you will place the second finger from the little finger, bent, in the same place. When you say three, you will similarly bend down the third. When you say four, you will likewise raise the little finger. When you say five, you will similarly raise the second from the little finger. When you say six, you will nevertheless raise the third as well, with only the middle finger, which is called the medicinal finger, fixed in the middle of the palm. When you say seven, with the rest raised, you will place only the little finger over the root of the palm. Next to it, when you say eight, place the ring finger. When you say nine, set the middle finger opposite it. When you say ten, you will fix the nail of the index finger in the middle joint of the thumb. When you say twenty, you will put the tip of the thumb between the middle joints of the index and middle fingers. When you say thirty, you will join the nails of the index finger and thumb in a gentle embrace. When you say forty, you will draw the inner parts of the thumb over the side or back of the index finger, with only those two held upright. When you say fifty, you will bend the thumb, curved like the Greek letter called gamma, toward the palm at the outer joint. When you say sixty, with the thumb curved as above, you will carefully encircle it from the front with the index finger bent around it. When you say seventy, you will fill the index finger, bent around as above, with the thumb stretched lengthwise, with only its nail raised across the middle joint of the index finger. When you say eighty, you will make the index finger bent around as above with the thumb held lengthwise on the left hand; two hundred on the right, in the same way as ten on the left, with it fixed in. But one hundred on the right is made in the same way as ten on the left. Likewise, one thousand on the right is as one on the left. Two thousand on the right, as two on the left. Three thousand on the right, with the fingers only raised toward the neck. When you say twenty thousand, you will place the same hand, widely spread out, upon the chest. When you say thirty thousand, with the same hand prone but upright, you will put the thumb against the cartilage of the middle of the chest. When you say fifty thousand, with the same hand prone but upright, the thumb...

You will place [the thumb] on the navel. When you say sixty thousand, with the same hand turned downward you will grasp the upper thigh from above. When you say seventy thousand, you will place the same hand upon the thigh. When you say eighty thousand, you will place the same hand, turned downward, upon the thigh. When you say ninety thousand, with the same hand you will take hold of the loins, with the thumb turned toward the groin. But from one hundred and two hundred thousand up to nine hundred thousand, you will complete them in the same order on the right side of the body. And when you say ten times one hundred thousand, you will intertwine both hands with the fingers interlaced. And so much for expressing numbers by the gesture of the fingers.

To these the same author soon adds: A certain manual speech can also be practiced from the very computation which I have set out, both for exercising the wit and for the sake of playing a game. By it, when the letters are expressed one by one, a person may convey to another who also knows this device, even if he is positioned far away, words composed of those same letters, so that they may be read and understood; or he may signify necessary things more secretly by these visible indications; or he may deceive the unskilled as if by divination. The order of this game or speech is as follows. When you wish to indicate the first letter of the alphabet, hold one with the hand; for the second, two; for the third, three; and so the rest in order. For example, if you wish to warn a friend placed among ambushers to act cautiously, show three and one, and twenty, and ten and nine, and five fingers; for the letters of this order signify, “act cautiously.”

Thus far the example of dactylogy according to Bede, which is also varied in many other ways. For suppose, as has also been said before, that the mark of unity signifies the letter a, and so on in order. Let one be placed on the thumb of the left hand, two on the index finger, three on the middle finger, four on the ring finger, or the third from the thumb, and five on the little finger. Likewise, on the right hand let two be understood on the thumb, three on the index finger, four on the middle finger, five on the third from the thumb, and six on the little finger. With these things so established, let us observe which numbers arise from the addition, multiplication, or division of which numbers among themselves. For example, twelve arises from the addition of one to eleven, two to ten, three to nine, four to eight, six to six, and seven to five. In multiplication, however, twelve is produced from the leading of four into three, or of two into six. In

division we have twelve if we divide twenty-four by two. Moreover, when the fingers alone are raised, this signifies addition; but when we touch one with another, multiplication. But if we bend one and raise the other, division must be understood. Therefore, wishing to show the letter m, which occupies the twelfth place, I indicate twelve either by addition, or by multiplication, or by division. First, with the two little fingers of both hands raised together with the thumb of the left hand, for the thumb signifies one, and one of the other fingers designates five, the other six; but five, six, and one make twelve, which number shows the letter m.

By multiplication it is done in this way: let us touch the third finger from the thumb of the left hand with the index finger of the right hand, since three multiplied by four makes twelve; or let us touch the little finger of the right hand with the index finger of the left, since likewise twice six yields twelve. It could also be done in another way, namely by the contact of the index finger of the right hand and the middle finger of the left, which show six. These, again, by the contact of both thumbs, or of the index finger of the right hand and the thumb of the left, signify multiplication of the former number by two; but twice six makes twelve.

By division, thus: first we shall indicate twenty-four, the division of which number by two gives twelve. Division by two is represented by the gesture of which I spoke above, namely if two thumbs are shown, one raised and the other bent; likewise the thumb and little finger of the left hand, and the index finger of the right hand bent. For they signify the division of six by three, that is, two, by which, when twenty-four is divided, they show twelve. So much for dactylogy, or the speech of the fingers, which can also be handled otherwise in countless ways, by assigning vowels, consonants, semivowels, double letters, and liquids to fixed places, and by treating such matters as each person shall see fit. Although these things may appear ridiculous, nevertheless they have very great use if they are transferred by a certain analogy to other matters. Moreover, there are some things of which the author makes mention partly in the exposition of this passage and partly near the end; but since they pertain to the treatment of steganography, let them be deferred for so long, until that point has been reached.

First kind of dermaticon. This stratagem is also commonly [unclear]

known to soldiers. Pliny, if I am not mistaken, gives another method in book 26. “Our people,” he says, “call tithymalus the milk-herb; others call it goat-lettuce.” They report also that when the body has been written on with its milk and it has dried, if ash is sprinkled on it, the letters appear; and in this way adulterers indeed preferred to communicate with one another rather than by little notes.

The second kind, Hyphasmaticon. The most learned man Theodorus Bibliander has hyphasmicon, for this reason, I think: in concealment of this sort no letters appear before the paper has been immersed in water. Thus, when we write letters with alum, water poured over them will make the paper darker than the letters, which otherwise could not have been read.

Letters are also written in various other ways. Herodotus, near the end of book 7: after Xerxes resolved to undertake an expedition against Greece, Demaratus, who was at Susa, learned of it and judged that it should be reported to the Greeks. But since he could not do it otherwise, for there was danger that he would be detected, he devised this plan: taking a pair of writing tablets, he scraped off the wax from them. Then he engraved the king’s plan on their wood. When the writing had been engraved, he covered it again with wax, so that the tablets being carried would cause no trouble with the guards on the roads. When they had been brought to Lacedaemon, the Lacedaemonians could not interpret them until, as I understand it, Gorgo, daughter of Cleomenes and wife of Leonidas, warned them and explained the matter itself, ordering the wax to be broken off, for then they would find the letters in the wood. Listening to her, the Lacedaemonians found the letters and read them, and then sent them on to the Greeks.

Gellius, book 17, chapter 9: “There is also,” he says, “in the records of Greek history another deep and unexpected hiding-place, devised by a barbarian stratagem.” There was a man named Histiaeus, born in a not undistinguished place in the land of Asia. King Darius then held Asia under his rule. When this Histiaeus was in Persia with Darius, he wished to announce certain secret matters to a certain Aristagoras by a furtive writing. He devised this hidden device for letters: from his slave, who had long had weak eyes, he shaved all the hair from the head

as though for the sake of healing him, and marked the smooth head into the forms of letters. In these letters he wrote out what he wished. Afterward he kept the man at home until the hair grew back. When this had happened, he ordered him to go to Aristagoras. “And when you have come to him,” he said, “tell him that I instructed him to shave your head, just as I myself recently did.” The slave came to Aristagoras as ordered and delivered his master’s message; and Aristagoras, thinking that the instruction was not pointless, did what had been commanded. In this way the letters were delivered.

Herodotus writes almost the same thing. In the same author, also, it is read in book 1 that when Astyages was harsh toward the Medes, Harpagus, insinuating himself with each of them, persuaded the leading men that Astyages ought to be removed from the kingship and Cyrus chosen. After these matters had been arranged and prepared, Harpagus, wishing at last to disclose his intention to Cyrus, who was among the Persians, but unable to do so otherwise, since the roads were guarded, devised a plan of this kind. He gutted a hare which he had obtained by skill, without cutting it open at all, and placed inside it a little book in which he had written what he wished. Sewing up the belly again, he gave the hare, together with nets, to one of his own household hunters, a most trustworthy man, and, instructing him orally that when he gave the hare to Cyrus he should tell him to open it with his own hands and to do this without witnesses, he sent the man away into Persia. When the messenger had carried this out, Cyrus received the hare, opened it, and read the little book found inside it. See Justin, book 1.

Historians also report that doves served as messengers in difficult affairs: letters tied to their necks or feet were sent during the siege of Mutina by Hirtius the consul to Decimus Brutus, and by Decimus Brutus to Hirtius. Food had been set out in certain very high places, and doves, first shut up in darkness and afflicted with great hunger, had been trained to fly back and forth from there.

Some, to avoid suspicion, write on paper with ink, as though they wished to tell a friend something about household affairs; afterward they write the secret matter in the spaces with urine. Others use the juice of lemons or onions; others use crushed sal ammoniac with water poured over it. Writings made with letters of this sort remain wholly hidden until they have been brought near fire. Some follow the poet’s advice: “Since he can hide papers tied to his leg, and [unclear].”

And, fastened beneath the foot, let her carry flattering notes. Let the guard beware of this; let her offer her conscious back in place of paper, and carry words on her own body. A letter made from fresh milk is also safe, and deceives the eyes; touch it with powdered charcoal and you will read it. That too deceives which is made with the point of a moist flax-thread; a little tablet brings hidden marks to light.

There are also other devices: for instance, they paint letters on flint with the fat of a goat or ox; when it has been placed in vinegar for several hours and then taken out again, it displays to sight what had been written on it. Likewise, they write with egg white and dip it into ink; when this is scraped off, the letters become visible. Finally, in this passage he has wrapped many things in obscure words not at all accepted in common usage, lest he give depraved people an opportunity either to misuse these things or to devise worse ones. He wrote race, with the syllables reversed, for cera, just as Roma for amor, nemilua for alumine, raphocam for camphora, etc. But since such matters must be handled rather sparingly for the public good, and do not belong to our undertaking, let us omit explaining everything. It is enough if it is understood what he wished to signify by this third kind of letters.

“There were also, as Bede attests)” The sense is this: the ancients not only wrote or spoke by words, as we do, but also, by a certain deliberate practice, transferred to the signification of things whatever the world contains and whatever can be comprehended by us. Diodorus Siculus, in book 4, says: “The letters of the Egyptians are very like various living creatures, the extremities of men, and tools, especially those of craftsmen. For their words are not expressed by the composition of syllables or by letters, but by the form of images, their meaning having been handed down to human memory by usage. They write, for example, a hawk, a crocodile, a serpent, a human eye, hands, a face, and other things of this sort. The hawk denotes a thing done quickly, since this bird is almost the swiftest of all; this notation is transferred to domestic affairs that are done swiftly. The crocodile signifies evil. The eye is interpreted as the preserver of justice and guardian of the whole body. Among the remaining parts of the body, the right hand with the fingers spread out denotes freedom,

but the left hand with the fingers clenched denotes graspingness and avarice.” In the same way, by the figure of the other parts of the body and by tools they marked some definite thing; and when these had been preserved in human memory by long usage and reflection, people recognized at once what they expressed.

Petrus Crinitus also, book 5, chapter 2, writes that this kind of method of writing existed among the Egyptians: “Concerning the letters of the Egyptians, which are called hieroglyphic, mention is found among the ancient authors, and this can still be observed on obelisks. On them those figures and images of various animals, plants, rivers, and trees are carved, and they designate the philosophy of that nation, as Strabo and Pliny, very weighty authors, testify. For on the obelisks of the kings Sesostris and Nuncoreus, which were brought from Egypt into the city, an interpretation of the nature of things was recorded by symbols of this kind and by hieroglyphic signs. Thus the philosophy of the Egyptians is believed first to have been made manifest, as is reported by the same Pliny and by others. Among other images they were accustomed to mark scarabs, bees, rivers, oxen, vultures, and other things of that sort. Moreover, from the very image of the bee the symbol of the king was signified, because he, in carrying out the duties of life, ought to have no less the sting of justice than the sweet clemency of honey. In the vulture they indicated the genius and majesty of nature, because among these birds females alone are found,” etc. They also painted many other signs in place of words; on these see Horapollo On Hieroglyphic Letters, Pliny book 36, chapter 8, and likewise chapter 12, where, according to the more correct reading, Sesostris is found for Sesotidis and Phaeron for Nuncoreus. Strabo, book 17, Cornelius Tacitus, book 13, Coelius Rhodiginus, Antiquarum lectionum book 29, chapter 26, and Volaterranus, book 33, also made mention of letters of this kind, although he writes that they have not yet been discovered by anyone.

“There were those who by accidents)” The meaning is this: whatever things exist in the whole nature of things, whether they are perceived by the intellect or by the senses, can be turned to this use, so that they signify in the same way as words. Hence it is that the intention of our mind may be signified to another secretly in countless ways, without suspicion and without hindrance from any person, through words,

through signs that denote words, as through light, through colors, shadows, sounds, odors, tastes, through qualities that affect touch, through shapes, sizes, numbers, through the motion or position of any things whatever, such as the parts of the body, through gestures of the fingers, nods of the eyes, and so forth. Indeed all these things, if they are handled rightly and arranged according to letters, syllables, words, and sentences, in a fixed order and with numbers assigned, provide human beings with remarkable powers, and powers so much more excellent as a person is more skilled and practiced in those disciplines that deal with the principles, causes, and accidents of sensible things. Such is catoptrics, which teaches how to present visible signs of things to sight in an instant, through certain images projected far from us, outside mirrors, into the air, and appointed to signify some sentence; these images are easily understood by one who has knowledge of the signs. But in what way it might be possible for all things to be transferred to the use of signs is not part of the present undertaking, but belongs to steganography. The very learned man Johannes Trithemius, in a certain letter to Bostius, recounts the contents of that work in these words, etc.

“I now have in hand a great work which, if ever it is published, which may it not be, the whole world will marvel at; the title of its first book is Steganographia. There will be four books, each divided into at least one hundred chapters. I began this work at the urging of a certain great prince, whom there is no need to name. You ask what this work teaches? It teaches very great things, astonishing and incredible to all who do not know them, things that have never been heard of since the beginning of the world. For the first book contains more than one hundred ways of writing secretly whatever you wish, without any suspicion, without transposition of letters, without any fear, so that there is no person in the world who by natural ingenuity could know or even suspect what is contained in my letters, except one who knows the art from me or from someone whom I have taught. The words are plain and familiar, lacking all suspicion; but no one will ever be able to perceive my intention without the art, however learned he may be, and it is a truly astonishing thing. The second book will contain things much more marvelous, namely by means of it, in this art, I can make the conception of my mind known to one who knows my art,

at any distance whatever, at a hundred miles or more, safely, without words, without writings, without signs, through any messenger whatever. If he is captured on the way, even if questioned under the harshest tortures, he can disclose nothing about my message, because he knows absolutely nothing about it. Whatever may happen, my message will always remain hidden, nor could all the people of the whole world, if they were gathered together, track it down by natural power. I can also do this without a messenger whenever I wish. I can also indicate my will to one sitting in prison who knows the art, even when I am far away, however much he is guarded, even if he were sitting three miles beneath the earth. And all these things I can do most broadly and universally, whenever and as often as I wish, naturally, without any superstition or aid of any spirits whatever. They are marvelous things, I admit; but hear things more marvelous.

“The third book teaches an art by which I can teach an uneducated man who knows only his mother tongue, and who has never known a word of the Latin language, within two hours to write, read, and understand Latin rather elegantly and eloquently, as much as he wishes, so that whoever sees his letters will praise the words and understand that they are composed in Latin. The fourth book contains many astonishing experiments, but purely natural ones. That is, I can indicate my mind to one who knows the art whenever I wish, even while speaking, preaching, playing the organ, or singing, without impediment to any other action, so that in preaching good and holy things I may indicate, not by words, not by signs, to anyone who knows the art, most broadly whatever I wish, even with eyes closed. And the fourth book will contain many other secrets, which are not to be brought before the public. All who hear these things marvel at them; among them are many noble and very learned men, who judge that these things are either impossible or wholly supernatural. To them, and to you, I reply what I have replied to many: that many things are naturally possible which, to those ignorant of the powers of nature, seem impossible or even supernatural. And behold, I speak before my God, who knows all things, that the marvelous things I have set forth are much more excellent, deeper, and greater than I can write or you can believe; and yet all are purely natural, without any deception, without superstition, without magical art, without invocation or service of any spirits whatever. I have said these things so that, if perhaps at some time a rumor should reach you that I either know or can do marvelous things, you would not, I say, think me a magician, but a philosopher. For what to Albertus

that because of the wonders he accomplished by the hidden power of nature, he was regarded by the common people as a magician; I am certain that the same thing can similarly happen to me. If you ask whence I have these things, which no one else knows, listen. I learned these things not from a man nor through a man, but through a revelation of I know not whom. For when in the present year I was at one time considering what new thing I might be able to discover that would be hidden from everyone, I began to consider whether I could devise those wonderful things I have described. After long imagining, when I had utterly despaired of it as an impossible matter, I put myself to sleep that night, laughing to myself at my own folly, since I had attempted to seek impossible things. That same night someone stood by me, saying, “The things you have thought are not vain, O Trithemius, although they are impossible to you, and although neither you nor anyone with you will be able to discover them.” And I said to him: “If, then, they are possible, tell me, I beg you, how they may be done.” And, opening his mouth, he taught me about each of them in order, showing how the things over which I had thought in vain for many days could easily be done. Behold, before God, since I do not lie but speak the truth, I have not yet taught these things to anyone, although many, promising great rewards, have often asked, except for one prince to whom I am writing, whom by a clear proof I have made more certain of the possibility of the art. Nor is it fitting for others to know these things than princes; otherwise many evils would be done through them: betrayals, deceptions, fornications, and whatever else evil men might wish. But those who use the art well could accomplish many good things for the republic through it. Moreover, I can teach all these things in every language of the whole world, even one I have never heard. These things, Bostius, I have wished to tell you for this reason, lest you think me idle.”

Thus far the words of Trithemius. Finally, there are other enormous advantages in these books of the Polygraphia, which we shall discuss in our books On the Method of Teaching and Learning; for however these things may appear, they have more in reserve than they promise on the surface. Concerning the Steganographia, in whose first books hidden matters lie concealed, with God’s will we shall treat separately.

We rejoice that the end of the first book of our Polygraphy is at hand; having been made readier for what remains, we judge that the powers of our talent should be tested. For newly discovered beginnings sometimes cause disturbance, because the one whom all follow has no one going before him. The first beginning of any invention is the more difficult; after it has been made firm, it brings greater confidence to its author. Therefore, completing with God’s favor and help the first book of our invention, we have divided the whole into three hundred eighty-four small units, assigning to each in order, as is seen, its own grades of periphrases. And these form a sufficiently beautiful Christian harmony: sixteen way-stations, with more than two hundred nine thousand phrases duly joined together in every respect.

Nothing is lacking here for students of these inventions of ours, so that in mystical, secret, and hidden matters, even in matters to be announced at a greater distance with the utmost security, they may have the fullest knowledge and faculty. All things that are contained in the sphere of the art proceed in circle and point; their atoms constitute a circular line, and, by the multitude of light, a straight one. Whatever is outside the line serves the common reckoning of day, not of night. For night, always enclosed within the limits of the small units and paraphrases, never goes out beyond them.

Therefore, whenever you cross the straight line of day and do not fulfill the purpose of the nocturnal syntax, turn the head back to the tail; and, when the connection has been made, let a binding of both with one another be made. Arrange the shadow in such a way that it does not confuse the sun by similarity of voice. And do not fear embarrassment if, in the first calculation, the day has not comprehended the shadow; rather, carefully consider the small units of the lines of day, and count one together with the other until the necessary proportion follows according to your wish. You will also be able to make a leap from the first into the second, knowing that in the first creation of days there was made evening and morning, one day. But when evening has been completed, bring this day back into the following one; and, when the sign has been given by the point, fix the mystery known at once to the binary and to the monad.

But so that you may be able to avoid this difficulty, distinguish the great revolutions of our whole circle by arithmetical degrees; and where day is repeated for night, place the mark of Archimedes upon the flying one, lest the immature ternary [unclear] return to unity.

For this reason we have set small divisions before the individual degrees by an artful invention, so that in these matters we might relieve the practitioner from the labor of numbering the periphrases. If you are industrious, diligent, and studious in those things that we have handed down as the principles of a new art, believe us: you will discover greater things lying hidden than we have promised. Indeed, since many natural secrets are contained in these matters, know this one thing, not the least: by the prudent operation of metathesis, whenever you wish, you will make even the most skilled person in this art ignorant, the seeing blind, and the learned unskilled. If the false opinion of the Hebrews were true, this invention of ours would give to each person among eighteen thousand worlds his own ways of writing and announcing, safely and secretly and most widely, whatever hidden things they wished in Latin.

END OF THE FIRST BOOK of the Polygraphy.

THE BEGINNING OF THE SECOND BOOK, OR CHAPTER, OF THE POLYGRAPHY OF JOHANNES TRITHEMIUS, ABBOT OF SPANHEIM, OF THE ORDER OF SAINT BENEDICT.

The reckoning method of mortals should imitate nature by art, since the monad admits no calculation. Therefore, although the arrangement of the preceding book of the Polygraphy, through the extension and metathesis of particulars, may suffice, as it were, for the universals of this art in infinite progressions of number, nevertheless a definite consideration has moved us to join a second book to the first. The condition of light in each is different, but night preserves the order of its course inviolate in both. The prudent reader, from these small inventions of ours, not polished quite to the rule, will easily be able to discover greater and more polished ones, if he flourishes in excellent talent. Whatever visible thing is placed in the whole circuit of the world offers ready support for the service of this new art of ours. Air and fire, water and earth, springs and rivers, trees and fruits, flowers and grasses, words and names, accident and substance, stones and sand, dung and filth, things and words, honorable and shameful matters, woods and metals, hard and liquid things, things existing and not existing, history and fable, beasts and dumb animals, men and beasts of burden, each and all things that speech can express or the mind can think, furnish the broadest field for our Polygraphy, and promise that the art, so far as it can be established among mortals, will be expanded without limit. For just as, from unity through the binary, the ternary generates a perfect number in the quaternary, so the completion of this invention, by the quaternary in the binary twice perfected, establishing the root, gives us an infinite number under the small signals of things and

For even if among us all our things are finite, nevertheless many things often occur which, because of the slowness of our understanding, seem infinite to us. Who will be able to count the drops of the sea? And who will penetrate the inscrutable heart of man? Just as finite and circumscribable number can be led onward by progression into infinity, so the arrangement of this art is enlarged immeasurably by varied transposition. Whatever is seen anywhere in the whole world conforms in every respect to our arrangement, nor is there anything known to us that is empty of mystery, if the method is understood from the teacher. But we, persuaded by reason, have settled upon the service of the binary, and briefly explain the smallest part of the whole. Nor is an occasion given us to raise our attempt to weightier matters; but if an acceptable occasion should be offered to us, we shall not refuse to make more excellent things clear to those who desire them. For it is written: Where there is no hearing, never pour out speech. Therefore, adding the second book of the Polygraphia to the first, we keep the same form and method, setting out in the light of day three hundred and eight paraphrases of simple progression for honorable remembrance of the most chaste Mother of God; if time had been favorably at hand, we could have given more graceful things, and, with sufficient broad unfolding, more extensive things. But studious posterity will easily provide both, so as to add brilliance to the material and sufficient progress to the form. The first inventor of any art transmits greater things to posterity, because, since the beginnings of an art are hard and unfamiliar, no subtle invention is found perfected from its origin. From Peapolis, which is also Herbipolis, a city of the eastern Franks, on the twelfth day of the month of February, in the year of the Lord 1508.

With the aid of our Lord Jesus Christ, savior of faithful souls, who lives in the sacred Trinity in unity with the Father and the Holy Spirit, threefold in persons and one God in substance, incomprehensible, almighty, and everlasting; from whom, in whom, and through whom every good, beautiful, and true thing proceeds, we have brought this second book of the Polygraphia to an end. To him be praise, honor, power, and glory: he who by the innocence of his death freed our race from the ruin of eternal perdition and, by perpetual mercy, opened the entrance to eternal life for all who believe in him with a pure conscience. Line by line we record three hundred and eight paraphrases, deliberately avoiding a more extended digression. For at the beginning of this little work it seemed enough to us if we had given those who wished it a reason to seek out fuller things, since both time and method failed us for them. Farewell, friendly reader. From Peapoli, on the penultimate day of the month of February, in the year of the Lord 1508.

END OF THE SECOND BOOK of the Polygraphia.

THE THIRD BOOK of the Polygraphia of Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Peapol, of the Order of Saint Benedict, begins.

What has confused the unity of language from the beginning of human creation? Was it not the division of bodies and the variety of minds? For as Truth declares in the Gospel: “Out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks.” For the tongue is the instrument for bringing forth those conceptions which the mind has inwardly thought within itself. Yet there are many ways of conveying the secrets of the mind to perception through this ministry, and their properties vary both by use and by art. Usage, introduced at pleasure, is common to many; art, however, to few. Finally, even the very unregulated practice of speaking, how much it has varied among the Germans alone in six hundred years, no one will readily estimate unless he has often reread Otfried, the monk of Weissenburg, in his poems in the German language. The sea flows and ebbs; human beings, once they die, do not return again to the present life. Customs succeed customs, and the vigor of mortal minds always declines toward softer things. Who today among the Germans, those ancient emulators of the Greeks, keeps knowledge of the old idioms? In the chronicles and ancient histories of the Franks, Hunibald, Doracus, and the other writers who preceded us by a thousand years mixed into their compositions many sayings, both in old verse and in prose, of the German speech; today these are understood by few. Why do I speak of ancient times, when our own idiom among the East Franks, Swabians, Bavarians, Rhinelanders, Mosellans, Cologne people, Saxons, and Thuringians undergoes notable variation every day? Human beings change in time, and customs vary;

minds change, and garments vary; the simplicity of languages is altered, and the ancient property of idioms varies, and nothing stable is found in human affairs. For there is a vicissitude of all things, and variety succeeds the simplicity of minds. Who will be able to reduce this perpetual flowing-away, so to speak, to the concord of unity? For times pass, as Scripture says, and knowledge will be manifold.

That we add a third book to the two preceding books of the Polygraphia has not lacked a special reason. For since the wills of human beings are varied, many methods are rightly given for honorable operations. In those former ones, day illuminates night; in these, however, day lacks light. There light leads shadow around in light; here, however, the blind illuminates the blind, and, existing and remaining without eyes, supplies in darkness the sight which he does not have. Here night perpetually darkens day with gloom, and one walking in darkness without light provides guidance for the blind. These paraphrases serve all human beings throughout the world, and in every language they transmit any secret safely, securely, and without danger to the cabalistic binary. Latin raises laughter among barbarians, and barbarism itself arouses suspicion among Latins. Yet it matters nothing, or little, since however great the suspicion may be, it will nevertheless contain every most secret mystery.

Let the diligent operator recall to mind the rules and precepts that we have handed down, lest he labor uselessly and in vain for himself and for others. For understanding is required, without which the usefulness of no art will stand. We have shown in a few things the path to the greatest things, and with finite things we have given a method for infinite things. From things given and received, greater things are easily prepared from crumbs. Reader, remember that the retrograde mark can be set in every place until you reach the mark of rest.

Farewell. From Peapol, on the first day of March, in the year of the Lord 1508.

What we promised at the beginning of the third book of our Polygraphia, for obtaining the shadow and likeness of a new gloss before those unskilled in it, we have fulfilled by way of example, with a sufficient saving of labor. We have entrusted the night, safely serving hidden matters, to be led by the shadows of paraphrases, and we have inserted the numbers in the order of four lines throughout, adapted for the use of those who wish to employ them. The places are degrees of minutiae, having three thousand one hundred fifty fixed positions, although, if you wish, there remain also infinitely many moments of the hours for concealing, in every nation and language of the world, whatever secret matter may occur. The circle, arising linearly from a point, whenever the night exceeds the image of light, you will be able to reduce as much as you wish and as much as will be needed to the path by which you have proceeded. If much of the night remains, reduce the dragon's tail to its original caudal point at the head. But the binary is made altogether certain from the marks and signs of unity. He who hungers much must labor much, so that he may have something to eat. Nor is there need of great labor to lead wherever you wish that which advances of its own accord. Here, therefore, we set the end to the third book of our Polygraphia, in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. Gentle reader, farewell. From Peapoli, on the seventh day of the month of March, in the year of our Lord Jesus Christ the Savior one thousand five hundred eight, in the eleventh indiction.

END OF THE THIRD BOOK of the Polygraphia.

JOHANNES TRITHEMIUS, ABBOT OF THE MONASTERY OF SAINT JAMES THE GREATER, APOSTLE, at Würzburg, formerly of Sponheim, of the order of Saint Benedict: the fourth book of the Polygraphia begins.

The order of reason required that the fourth book of our Polygraphia be made unlike the preceding books in quality, invention, and ease, so that those who wish to share in the secrets of our matters may attain this not by one way, but by various and diverse ways. We have extended the pica, comprehensible by a very easy invention, so that night, always joined by the minute to the monad, may in any order be recognized in the light of day. Here no disagreement is found between unity and the binary; nor will one who wishes to perform the art need to have the instrument of the art at hand, since what succeeds the first without an intermediary shows the hidden mystery. Hence a prudent man, understanding and experienced in the science, will satisfy the operation at every time and place. The binary receives from unity, whence it produces the ternary. The recognition of this cryptology is easy at first sight, after the moon has been illuminated by the sun, even by a single point. And yet it may happen that the knower becomes skilled without the guiding hand of a teacher. I think, however, that this is to be understood only in this book, and in none of the preceding ones. Concerning those that follow, judgment will be given in its proper place. Among all the cabalistic methods of secrets that we have given up to the present, the procedure of this fourth book, easier than the rest, can be extended to infinity. Therefore it is enough that I have handed down to those desiring fuller things both the form and the reason of the example.

The light of understanding easily penetrates all these things. I wrote at Peapolis, on the ninth day of March, in the year of the Lord 1508.

Now that the demonstration of the possibility of our new invention has been shown rather briefly and yet sufficiently, I do not think that I myself should be wearied any longer over the same matter at this time, since the method provides a road onward to infinity, if anyone should need a model for further things. Nor do I think it at all necessary to recall to memory the matters recited in the preceding pages, since a discerning reader, if he is diligent, will also be able, with the Lord’s help, to discover the greater things that lie hidden in these. We have given the material, and at the same time the occasion, to the wise and diligent man; if he wishes to use them prudently, he will surpass our ingenuity with his own. But whoever wants this road to be more beautiful in its shade should join hand and mind to ingenuity, and make for himself a path more beautifully adorned by paraphrase. If these things delight anyone, let him keep it fixed in memory that he must always remain within the appointed circle; if he transgresses it in any way, the whole operation vanishes as useless. There are many names of men; indeed, there are almost infinite terms for things, villages, cities, provinces, trees, stones, and words, all of which serve our purposes. From these it is clear that it is not impossible for a book and a method to be made, provided that intelligence is at hand with diligence, which would surpass our inventions without limit. But the man who is of such dullness that he cannot understand these childish things of ours, when will he penetrate the subtler things that remain? We place an end upon the fourth book of the Polygraphia, to which, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, we join the fifth.

END OF THE FOURTH BOOK of the Polygraphia.

JOHANNES TRITHEMIUS, ABBOT OF SAINT JAMES THE APOSTLE AT PEAPOLIS. The Fifth Book of the Polygraphia The Beginning of the Chapter.

Those matters which, with the help of our Lord Jesus Christ, we have set out in some fashion in the four preceding books for the completion of our Polygraphia reasonably require that, in the fifth book, we briefly treat the remaining precepts and methods of this same instruction that still remain. Accordingly, in it we shall give a sufficiently concise method by metathesis, that is, by transposition of letters, by which a friend may write safely, securely, and most secretly to a friend whatever he wishes. We read that Caesar Augustus used this method of writing in secret matters. Although this method of communicating is indeed secure in many ways, it is nevertheless always regarded with suspicion by those who look at it, because as soon as the transposition of the letters is perceived, anyone who is inquisitive at once suspects that something lies hidden under them. Now the methods of this invention are almost infinite; from them, for a necessary introduction, we have marked out the following for the reader, while reserving the rest to be searched out by his own ingenuity. First, therefore, we have set before him the canonical table of this art, and below it we have written another, reversed. In these two tables the root and foundation of the aforesaid transposition is altogether placed, and upon it the structure of the whole edifice is set. For once these two tables have been properly known and understood, no transposition of letters will be able to escape the diligent practitioner. To these we have joined twenty-four alphabets in order, so that we might provide the reader with an abundance of ways to transpose letters. The use of these lies, as one chooses, either in individual alphabets or, if you prefer, in all of them. If you have secret dealings with many people, distribute the individual alphabets to your individual associates, but commit to memory what you have given to each one.

[unclear]

d

[unclear]

...you have handed it on. First, indeed, let the first alphabet be entrusted to the first person, the second to the second, the third to the third, and so on likewise with the rest. But if, because of the multitude of business or of one's household, the alphabets which we have indicated should not suffice for everything, or if some of them seem too open and obvious, we shall be able to introduce various new transpositions, of which the number may be very great, while the method of the secret always remains hidden. Let us set down an example of this: let B be a, f be b, l be c, p be d, t be e, z be f, c be g, m be h, and so on through the whole usual alphabet, so that between any adopted letter three letters lie idle and transposed. Afterward let there be four, then five, more or fewer, yet in such a way that the whole alphabet, as though revolved into a circle, comes together, and no letter is omitted at all, but each is placed in the same sequence for another in its own order. In whatever way you write it, you must know that it is to be entrusted firmly either to writing or to memory, lest, through a lapse of forgetfulness, you yourself can no longer read what you have written.

For the transposition of letters can be varied in as many ways as, according to the estimation of the human intellect, which, enclosed in temporal operation in a mortal body, does not properly grasp infinities, there will arise a mortal number that is innumerable. Therefore whoever wishes to have more methods of writing by metathesis, and methods remote from our instruction, if he is even a little ingenious and diligent, will easily attain the desired effect in his operation. For the ingenuity of a person can do very great things if it is aided by study and art. But he who despises the smallest things will never reach the greater. I know that many will come who will deride these studies of ours as vain and childish; to them we give as our answer that we shall be wholly content, provided they please those at whose request they have been composed by us.
