In the present orchema a multiple alphabet is handed down by transposition and leap, both according to the rule of order and according to the position of the letters. All these things will suffice as an example for those who cannot be content with the examples already set down, so that they may have a method and form for discovering the remaining ones, since they can be varied without number.

JOHANNES TRITHEMIUS, ABBOT PEPOLITANUS, greets the reader.

Since all the letters of the Greeks and the Hebrews are numerical, I have often wondered that the curious Latin learning of the ancients did not also make its own letters serve the reckoning of numbers. The Hebrews, by doubling certain letters, established twenty-eight letter-signs, sufficient for every number. The Greeks, however, relieved this lack of letters by adding four characters, with similar foresight. Since we, therefore, have twenty-four letters, why do we not also make ours numerical, since we can likewise find four doubled forms? Let us give four as an example, and there will be enough for every number: m and final ij; likewise r and final t; likewise long s and final or closed s; likewise closed v and open u. When we join these to the twenty-four usual letters, we have twenty-eight characters, sufficient for all numbers. Nor will it be a matter of great labor to grasp this method of numbering for those who already know the letters, if they have once committed it to memory. For this invention of ours will be useful to many, since in a few letters it comprises many thousands in number, all of which can be discerned and understood at first glance, without any calculation, more clearly than daylight. Many people, especially those less experienced in the art of calculation, think that this cannot be done so easily by means of algorismic figures, particularly in large numbers. For as soon as you have looked with your eye at a number, however large, you will be able both to understand it fully and to express it without circumlocution or division of speech. So that this may be done easily, it is fitting that we set down the letters themselves reduced to number. Written on 16 March, in the year 1508.

The sixth book of the Polygraphy of Johannes Trithemius, abbot of Saint James the Greater, Apostle, at Würzburg, begins.

Before every invention and use of letters, at the beginning of the world, when human beings were still rude in intellect and uncultivated in habits, under the administration of a threefold alternation, as some think, of intelligences succeeding one another in order through 1,063 years, the influences of the planets in the sphere held sway in their own manner over bodies on earth. The ancient investigators of this matter say that Saturn, from the beginning of the world, presided by his influence over things germinating and growing on earth, chiefly through his governing intelligence, whom they called Orisiel, that is, the life-giving one of God, for 354 lunar years, likewise four months, and as many days and hours. These things we report as poetic, but we do not affirm them.

After Saturn, Venus is said to have assumed rule; after Venus, Jupiter. After Jove, Mercury, the fourth ruler in order, adorned human minds with various arts. Under the three intelligences just mentioned, that is, while Saturn, Venus, and Jove were ruling, they assert that human beings had no use or knowledge of letters. Therefore, whenever one person wished to announce some secret matter to another, he did this not in writing, since the service of letters was lacking, but symbolically, by certain likenesses of animals, trees and plants, or of other sensible things, according as each had agreed among themselves.

The time of Saturn, as they say, gave human beings habits properly corresponding to its influence. For it made them farmers, hunters, founders of cities, rude, forest-dwelling, gloomy, simple, uncultivated in life and habits,

f iij

and living for a long time in the flesh. After Orifiel of Saturn, as those who hold such opinions say, the intelligence Anael, the mover of Venus, received the governance of the world by influence and continued it for 354 years, and for four months, days, and hours. Under him human beings began to be more cultivated, to build houses and cities more frequently, and also to invent various manual arts, namely the work of weaving, wool-working, and many other things like these. They also began to sink more deeply into the pleasures of the flesh, to take beautiful wives, and, after many children had been begotten from them, they notably fell away from their natural simplicity. They invented games and songs, began to play the cithara, and more eagerly devised whatever they affirm belongs to the influence of Venus, following too much the movement of the flesh.

They named the third intelligence of Jupiter Zachariel. Taking up the dominion of the world after Anael, he made human beings restless with desire for rule, made them engage in hunting, make tents, and adorn themselves with various garments. While he was ruling, in accordance with the character of Jupiter, who deprived his father of the kingdom, a great division arose between the good and the wicked: the former calling upon God, the latter given over to the flesh and the world. Under this governance Adam, the first man, died, leaving to all posterity the testament of dying once.

The fourth mover, or angel, of Mercury, Raphael, after Zachariel, began to exert influence upon worldly affairs in the 1055th year of the world, at the end of the month of February, and lasted until the 1410th year of the world. Under him the use of letters is said to have been invented first. The letters then, as they report, were quite different from those that the world has today, devised according to the form and likeness of trees, plants, and animals; yet with time they were afterwards changed in many ways, and took on an easier mode of formation and a more cultivated adornment. For the fictions of the poets said that Mercury was the patron of all literature, promising that great hidden mysteries of things lay beneath their stories.

After this, when the human race had multiplied and spread everywhere over the whole earth, the unity of letters did not long remain. Rather, the separation of bodies and minds far from one another discovered diverse and various modes of writing, concerning which the account would be long for us. Plato the philosopher, in the Phaedrus, says that letters and the use of writing,

together with the theory of weights and numbers and the game of dice, were first invented by a certain philosopher named Theuto, and that he taught them to Thamus, king of the Egyptians. But concerning the rest of the ancient men who are said to have given special letters to nearly individual nations and peoples, which remain in their use down to the present day, it is not my purpose on this occasion to set down or mark out an account.

For all the more learned men of our time know that Cadmus, son of Agenor, king of the Phoenicians, is said first to have brought sixteen letters into Greece: α. β. γ. δ. ε. ζ. ι. λ. μ. ν. ο. π. ϱ. σ. τ. ψ. To these Palamedes, at the time of the Trojan War, is reported to have added four: ξ. θ. φ. χ. And Pythagoras afterwards added the letter θ, so that they would be twenty-one. χ. κ. ω. were subsequently invented by others. Jordanes, bishop of the Goths, gave letters proper to his people.

When the unity of language had been confused, the simplicity of characters too was varied in many ways. Hence it came about that the use of letters, in the course of time, claimed such great license for itself that not only individual peoples, but also individual men, fashioning new characters for letters at their own discretion, prepared hiding places for their mysteries. Yet every writing in an unusual character will not be free from suspicion among those who see it. Notwithstanding this, kings, tyrants, and many ancient princes once discovered for themselves a familiar mode of writing set apart from the common one, taking thought for the suspicion of others, provided that what they wished to remain secret was not perceived.

In imitation of these, I too, though very well known, and desiring to bring this work of Polygraphy, as far as possible, to a perfect conclusion, have resolved in this sixth and final book to recall from the underworld certain characters of the ancients which have now ceased from the use of mortals, lest they perish entirely. And first indeed we shall set forth the ancient mode of writing of the Northmen.

CONCERNING THE ALPHABET AND THE MARVELOUS MODE of writing of the Northmen, at the time when they were laying waste Gaul by their incursion.

All the letters of the Greeks and Palestinians are numerical, as was said earlier, whereas among the Latin letters, which we Germans also use, only seven are counted as numbers, namely c, d, i, l, m, v, and x.

The Northmen, together with the Asiatic Dacians, once came out from the Scandinavian islands, which are now called Gothic, and for more than forty years, roaming through Gaul, devastated it very severely. In order to look after their secret affairs, as Bede the English monk testifies, they devised the following new and elegant mode of writing from Greek letters. For they adapted the Greek numbers, comprised in ten letters up to twenty-four, to Latin characters, and prudently concealed our letters under a foreign form, that is, in the way in which we use numbers in place of letters, when, for example, we put 1 for a, 2 for b, 3 for c, 4 for d, and so on in sequence to the end of the alphabet.

It was indeed an elegant and sufficiently safe invention, which neither a Greek nor a Latin would easily understand. For the whole alphabet is not found in it, but only nine letters and one numerical sign, namely g, which among them signifies six and in this mode of writing represents f, the sixth letter of the Latins. Moreover, yielding to our German language in which we were born, we have added double w at the very end in place of the twenty-fourth letter of our nation, which we have formed according to the Greek number in this way: kΛ. We shall set out this writing of the Northmen in imitation of them, according to the following order of Greek letters.

A α 1 B β 2 C γ 3 D δ 4 E ε 5 F θ 6 G ψ 7 H χ 8 I ι 9 K κ 10 L λ 11 M μ 12 N ν 13 O ζ 14 P π 15 Q q 16 R σ 17 S τ 18 T υ 19 U φ 20 V χ 21 X ψ 22 Y η 23 Z ξ 24

By the aid of this alphabet the Northmen wrote with secure transmission whatever they wished to keep hidden among themselves. No Greek could understand this method of writing, since, although all these characters are Greek, nevertheless, because they represent Latin letters according to numerical order, they could be read neither by a Greek nor by a Latin who had not previously acquired knowledge of this technique.

This method of writing can also be varied in many ways, when the numbers and letters are changed by metathesis. This can also be done with complete Greek letters, according to the wish and judgment of any industrious writer. Nor will the manner of forming these characters be very difficult, especially for someone who has had a little practice. The characters written above are also quite suited to the German language, since with them we can mark down everything that occurs to us, in whatever speech we are skilled. Whenever iota is placed by itself, so that it may be known to denote the letter l, the tenth of the alphabet, it is marked above in this way: ī.

ON THE ALPHABET AND METHOD OF WRITING OF THE ANCIENT FRANKS.

[unclear]

It is the opinion of very many that the Germans once had letters from the Greeks, and they steadfastly affirm that they also used the Greek language, especially in their sacred rites. For they say that a great kinship between the Greek language and ours has now been utterly extinguished. That most learned man, my former teacher Johannes Camerarius Dalburgius, most reverend bishop of the church of Worms, had collected several thousand Greek words which mean the same thing in both languages, Greek and German. And Caesar testifies in the Commentaries that the Druids, the ancient priests of sacred rites in Gaul, used the Greek language, especially in sacred matters. But when the Romans were ravaging the world, they at last violently imposed the use of their own letters, together with their dominion, upon many nations. Finally the remnants of the Trojans, who were afterward called Franks, in the four hundred fortieth year after the Incarnation, from the borders of the Scythians—

[unclear]

with King Marcomer providing leadership, and came into Germany; and from their brothers the Saxons they received settlements at the mouths of the Rhine. Thereafter, for nine hundred and fifty years, waging almost continual war with the Romans and the Gauls, as Hunibald is the authority, they finally brought nearly all Europe under their empire or kingdom. Yet, once they had accepted the letters of the Romans, they did not abolish them; rather, being themselves mingled among Germans and Gauls, they learned their language and preserved their letters and the form of their writing. Vuasthaldus, a writer of the histories of this people, wrote in his native language books of the deeds of kings, dukes, and princes over almost seven hundred and fifty-eight years, adding, as Hunibald says, the characters which he mentions in his volume, which he published in eighteen books on the origin of the Franks.

Λ ζ χ θ υ ν β φ ρ ψ λ γ ω ϕ Δ δ κ π Ξ ξ λ σ Ε ɛ μ τ

Unless a scribe’s error has deceived me, I have represented Vuasthaldus’s alphabet suitably, as I think. In it some characters differ altogether from the Greek ones, while some seem partly to resemble them. Yet I do not know what to judge: whoever their inventor was, although he did not preserve the form of the Greek letters, he did observe the order of the letters. The codex, perishing from excessive age, could scarcely be read; hence I fear that I have rather been deceived by some interpolator than discovered Hunibald’s true and certain meaning.

But let us pass on to what remains, since if Hunibald’s statement is true, it will have been well written by us; but if it is someone’s fiction, it will neither harm us nor do the reader an injury. Another fictitious alphabet follows, found in Hunibald’s codex, to which this was written as a heading.

THE ALPHABET OF THE FRANKS, which Doracus invented.

Whoever wishes to use the characters written above should know that they must be written below the lines, in the manner of the Greeks, not above, as the Latins do. Likewise it should be observed that, among doubled letters, the first forms are written at the beginning and in the middle of words, but the second forms always at the end.

FROM THE GRAMMATICAL WORKS OF OTFRID, monk of Weissenburg.

I have read that Charles, king of the Franks, surnamed the Great, taking pity on the barbarism of his nation, with Nanno, Theobald, Albinus, and Berenger as helpers, attempted to regulate the German language. And when, as Turpin testifies, he had begun so difficult a work, he was held back by frequent incursions of wars and did not complete it, but, forestalled by death, left it unfinished; nor did another arise after him who would call the care of this matter to mind. But Otfrid,

the monk already mentioned, once the hearer and disciple of Rabanus of Fulda, under Louis the Pious, the son of that Charles, having obtained that grammar, though imperfectly, wrote many things in our German language which seem to sound with a remarkable dignity of regular instruction. For he composed many poems according to that same norm, in both heroic and elegiac meter; furthermore, he composed some things in prose for Louis, king of Germany, son of Louis the Pious and brother of the emperor Lothar; also for Otgar, archbishop of Mainz, for the monks of St. Gall, and for others. Having also obtained fragments of this grammar, I have extracted the present characters of the alphabet from many others, lest they should utterly perish. It is established, on Otfrid’s testimony, that Charles devised several alphabets of his own, which he used securely throughout his very broad kingdom in secret matters with individual prefects. From these, with Otfrid serving as our guide, we commit a few things to these letters.

Zι ϒ Ρ 7 B Φ λ Ι O 6 V Κ μ Π R 2 X Π φ Λ Q 9 Y Σ π Ψ T Z Ψ m ψ U

King Charles the Great, the most Christian emperor, fought for thirty years with the Saxons, whom at last, overcoming them by the sword, he converted to the Christian faith. But fearing that they might again, as they had done many times, apostatize from the faith, he appointed certain secret investigators, to whom he granted judicial authority. They were to travel through all Saxony and secretly inquire diligently into the faith and conduct of the people; and whomever they found to have apostatized from the faith, or to be robbers, adulterers, blasphemers, or [unclear] of the church or its priests

...despisers of him and of his commands, or those who disturbed the Christian commonwealth by notorious crimes, or recalled or solicited the people to paganism, should without delay, by imperial and royal authority and without penalty, be hanged with a noose, or otherwise killed as they could be. And so that this institution might remain perpetually unshaken, he gave those same men power to appoint others also, suitable under certain conditions, who, enjoying the aforesaid authority, might exercise without penalty the office of inquiry and of death against the guilty. Finally, he prescribed for them secret laws, hidden signs, and at the same time the form of an oath, by which they might proceed justly in judging and punishing, and, known to one another, remain hidden from others, and preserve forever in greater secrecy the necessary judgment in the Saxon land. They also used certain alphabets among themselves for a time, though these at last fell entirely out of use. Yet the office of this kind of inquisition remains down to the present time; its ministers are commonly called Feimeri.

Yet continued practice in writing will be able, with easy compensation, to correct this misshapen crookedness, and frequent use will make it pleasing by habit.

I have also found another alphabet, newly devised by a certain alchemist, which he was accustomed to use in concealing his secrets, making great the estimation of his art, which contains little in itself except words. For alchemy is loved by many, and is chaste.

[alphabet, as printed]

a b c d e f g h i k l m n o p q r s t v x y z w

Alchemy has many household servants, who guard their mistress with continual vigilance and put themselves forward in her name, so that they may preserve her forever untouched by the intercourse of so many importunate lovers. Vanity, fraud, deceitfulness, deception, sophistic falsification, greed, falsehood, lying confidence, folly, want, poverty, despair, flight, outlawry, and beggary are alchemy’s handmaids. Pretending to be the beloved mistress, they keep her inviolate, and willingly prostitute themselves to her seekers: the moneyed, the avaricious, the greedy, and the silly.

ON THE SIGNS AND WONDERFUL METHOD, BUT ONE TOO LABORIOUS, OF WRITING OF M. T. CICERO, AND AFTER HIM OF SAINT CYPRIAN, BISHOP AND MARTYR.

Marcus Tullius Cicero, the eloquent orator of the Romans, wrote a book of signs of no small size, which Saint Cyprian, prelate of the Carthaginians and martyr, enlarged with many signs and words,

adding terms necessary for Christian uses, so that the work itself became useful not only to pagans but much more also to the faithful.

The codex is rare and was found by me only once, and bought at a low price. For when, in the year of the Lord’s nativity 1496, I was looking through many libraries out of love for books, I found this memorable codex in a certain monastery of our order, neglected because of its extreme age, cast aside under dust and despised. I asked the abbot, a doctor of law, how much he valued it. He replied that he would prefer to it the small works of Saint Anselm, lately printed. I went to the booksellers, since the matter occurred in a metropolitan city; I bought the requested small works of Anselm for one sixth part of a florin, gave them to the rejoicing abbot and monks, and rescued the codex, which was already almost brought to destruction. For they had determined, out of desire for the parchment, to destroy it.

Having been admitted by Johann Geiler of Kaysersberg, the distinguished preacher of that place, into the library of the greater church, I found an entire Psalter written in these same signs of Tullius and Cyprian, and most fittingly written with golden capitals. But an inscription of this sort had been placed on the outside by someone ignorant of the mystery: “Psalter in the Armenian language.” I summoned the doctor, showed the falsity, and warned that it should be rewritten: “Psalter written in Ciceronian signs.”

Whether he did so or not I am uncertain, since I did not afterwards return to that library. So that you may see, reader, the form of Cicero’s notation, we have decided to add a few signs below.

[sign] approves [sign] modest epistle [sign] approves together [sign] immodest letter [sign] disapproves [sign] moderate syllable [sign] upright [sign] immoderate h [sign] uprightness [sign] suitable time [sign] dishonesty [sign] accommodates through time [sign] acceptable [sign] in the manner temporal [sign] rejects [sign] according to the manner extemporaneous [sign] measure [sign] in what manner man

This method of writing requires a great memory and an utterly immense labor of reading, where any given character signifies either a whole word, or a final syllable, or some part of speech suitable for composing the whole. Therefore, setting aside all the signs, let us draw an alphabet from a few.

[alphabet of signs]

Many other new alphabets could also be formed from Cicero’s signs; we leave their extraction to the discretion of anyone who wishes to undertake it. For the book is abundant, and contains many signs notably differing from one another, all of which serve those who write.

[alphabet of signs]

This was the alphabet of Iaimiel, great king of the Articians, surnamed Megalopius, a most wise man, which he used in secret matters; and it too can be changed in many ways. To it, out of love for the prince, we have added this alphabet of ours below, in which, once it is used more frequently over time, the scribe will become more fluent.

[alphabet of signs]

HOW WE MAY ALSO WRITE ANY SECRETS SAFELY WITH NUMBERS AND IN MANY OTHER VARIOUS WAYS.

These things are childish, I admit, since anyone, according to his own capacity and judgment, could devise many more attractive alphabets than we have recorded in this volume. Therefore we knowingly omit many things which, for the same reason, we judge to be childish, common, and of little utility. We fear that someday we shall be ashamed to have applied our mind to these trifles while more useful matters were left aside. But I pray that readers will pardon me, since my own will indeed drew me back from these childish studies, not to say studies at least partly vain; yet the insistence of certain friends compelled me to write them, friends whom I could not refuse without injury to the bond between us. Nevertheless, persuaded by their entreaty, I have also decided to join the following chapter to those already set forth, and to put numbers in place of letters. For the ancients devised various and manifold ways of writing by means of number-figures. Accordingly, persuaded by the prayers of friends, we have placed at the end of this sixth book a few methods out of many, by which a path lies open to the knowledge of others, even for those who do not know them. For if anyone takes delight in knowing these things, once they are known he will easily be able to ascend to higher things, and to vary the methods discovered by manifold alternation according to his own judgment. As a beginning for this matter, we have set down a table under an orchema, which, when the reading is varied in the form of a cross, will contain within itself ninety-six alphabets.

The Sixth

With God’s mercy we have brought the sixth and last book of our Polygraphy to its end. In it, as we conclude our discourse with the wandering stars, we give the reader warning on certain points. First, whenever he uses the alphabet of any sign or planet, he should prudently add the character or mark of the same, for a double advantage. For by this means excessive labor will be removed from the friendly reader, and the mystery will remain secret, since anyone ignorant of the art will think that a table written in numbers and marked beforehand with the characters of signs or planets belongs to the reckoning of astronomy, and will suspect no hidden mystery at all. For this reason we have taken up the official matter for the letters not from one, but from a distance, so that we might give no one a mark of suspicion. Nevertheless prudence must be used by writers, since an astute reader touched by suspicion of something hidden, if he detects the function of one number, will easily calculate the whole alphabet.

Second, remember, whoever desires to be a shrewd practitioner of this matter, that whenever a letter is doubled in any word, as often happens, it should be written only once and marked above with a point. For example, I wish to write Ioannes from the alphabet of Aries: I do not duplicate 18, which is n, but write thus: 14. 16. 7. 18. 10. 23.; or abbas: 6. 7. 6. 23. Ioannes, abbas, so that every mark of suspicion may be removed. In similar cases one must proceed with similar caution, because unless the operator is endowed with diligence and knows how to discover greater things from small ones, he will not be fit for these least matters of ours to be disclosed to him. Not all things are to be communicated indiscriminately to everyone, especially those whose use can be turned to good and to evil.

Moved reasonably by that consideration, we have openly handed down many things in these six books of Polygraphy to those wishing to know, but we have allowed far more secret things to lie hidden beneath what is manifest. Finally, we have written a key that explains the whole work, showing how it is to be understood in each metaphor; yet, by the counsel of certain persons, we have ordered it to remain hidden at home, so that studious persons may not lack material for exercising their memory, and so that the rejected may be deprived of the occasion for knowing things they are not willing to use well. In every passage many mysteries lie hidden, and the greater the things you discover from these, the greater still are those that remain to be discovered. A path is prepared for beginners, on which, for those setting out,

it will not be difficult in the course of time to discover many things, both small and very great. Here a man who did not know how will learn to write Latin, and prudently to wrap all the mysteries of his will in a foreign speech. But in order that the unlearned man may be able not only to understand his own mysteries that he has wrapped up, but also plain speech, of which until now he has always been ignorant, the matter is not one of great labor, if the paraphrast has fully grasped our intention in this volume. For beneath the bark lie the kernels of our Steganography, buried for a just reason, lest they be open to unworthy babblers. In short, it was worthwhile that one work should not prejudice the other, but that its own right should be distributed to each inviolate.

We, wearied after a long voyage, here cast anchor in the sea under the name of JESUS CHRIST, Savior of the faithful, on the twenty-first day of the month of March, in the year of the Lord’s nativity 1508, the eleventh indiction of the Romans, at Pæapolis, a city of the eastern Franks, which they also call Würzburg and Herbipolis.

END OF THE POLYGRAPHY OF JOHANNES Trithemius, Abbot at Saint James in Würzburg, formerly of Sponheim, of the order of the divine father Benedict.

CORRECTION.

The fair reader must be warned that the order of the books of this Polygraphy is above all to be observed, lest the division of the signature that occurred in the first alphabet perhaps produce an error. There, indeed, the Key of the Polygraphy ends at c; after the remaining books, however, the Fifth Book begins again at d.

Frankfurt, from the workshop of Cyriacus Jacob.

YEAR 1550.

COR IRE DOMIN GREG VIA M

COR RE DEO MINI. G I S I N A N A W

1555. I am the book of Hieronymus [unclear].
